When SCP is terminated based on feasibility, the runtime is further reduced while the learned prior suppresses the severe high-cost tail observed with heuristic initialization. These results demonstrate that learned warm-starts can reduce onboard optimization cost while steering SCP toward basins containing feasible, low-cost solutions.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Simultaneous Forward and Inverse Human-in-the-Loop Optimization
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Kyeongwon Park, Steven H. Collins
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper introduces SFIHILO, a method that simultaneously optimizes human preferences and control policies in human-robot interaction, enhancing efficiency and adaptability through active querying.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Subjective user experience is important to human-robot interaction, but the outcomes users value, and how those preferences vary across individuals and contexts, are often unknown. While inverse learning approaches using human data can help identify user rewards, in many assistive settings the experimental costs of executing a control policy, measuring biomechanical or physiological outcomes, and collecting user feedback often limit the number of queries and optimization iterations. Here, we present Simultaneous Forward and Inverse Human-In-the-Loop Optimization (SFIHILO), which efficiently infers individual-specific reward functions from preferences over human outcomes and identifies a final control policy that maximizes the learned reward. SFIHILO bootstraps a forward model to predict user outcomes from control policies, uses this model for active querying to accelerate inverse reward learning, and then optimizes the final control policy without additional user trials. We score candidate policies by their expected reduction in uncertainty across both forward and inverse beliefs, targeting a regional preference boundary to robustly inform this simultaneous learning process. In simulation, we show that SFIHILO was effective across user heterogeneity, outcome dimensionalities, precision requirements, noise levels, and nonstationarity; compared with mutual information approaches, the proposed active querying strategy significantly improved sample efficiency in inverse learning while preserving forward model accuracy. This approach demonstrates the potential to infer latent human goals, enabling more transferable and effective human-robot interaction.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Self-Organizing Agent Teams Learn to Reason Together
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Aneesh Pappu, Mirac Suzgun, Yongchan Kwon, Federico Bianchi, Batu El
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: Self-Organizing Agent Teams (SAT) enable AI agents to collaboratively learn reasoning strategies, enhancing problem-solving accuracy through adaptive organization and communication.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Collective intelligence depends not only on what team members know, but also on how they organize their work. When the structure of a solution is unknown, useful roles and divisions of labor cannot be specified in advance; teams must learn from experience how to organize reasoning as it unfolds. Human teams routinely adapt this way, while existing AI agent teams rely on fixed protocols, explicit task decomposition, or routing. We introduce Self-Organizing Agent Teams (SAT), fixed teams of AI agents that learn reusable strategies from prior collaborations to organize roles, conversational phases, participation, and information flow. These strategies enable what we call collaborative computation: agents exchange, challenge, repair, and synthesize partial reasoning into solutions no member produced independently. In two independent settings, we learn teamwork strategies that transfer unchanged to unseen benchmarks, using only 15 mathematics and 25 graduate-level knowledge problems. Across five mathematics and physics benchmarks, self-organizing teams average 66.7% accuracy, versus 48.8% for their strongest member, 58.7% for compute-matched inference by that agent, and 59.0% for a perfect router over members' independent answers; on AIME 2026, they exceed this router by 13.4 points. Because gains vary across benchmarks, we ask when self-organizing collaboration helps. Across eight benchmarks, demonstrability (the organizational-psychology construct of whether a team can distinguish correct from incorrect reasoning) strongly tracks improvement over the strongest member (Spearman $ρ=0.90$, $p=0.005$): teams benefit most when correct reasoning can be recognized once it appears. More broadly, these results suggest that organization itself can become an agent capability: agent teams can learn how to reason together and produce solutions their members could not reach independently.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: HumanAgencyBench: Scalable Evaluation of Human Agency Support in AI Assistants
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Benjamin Sturgeon, Daniel Samuelson, Jacob Haimes, Jacy Reese Anthis
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper presents HumanAgencyBench, a diagnostic tool assessing AI assistants' support for human agency, revealing varied effectiveness across behaviors and developers.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: As humans delegate more tasks and decisions to artificial intelligence (AI), we risk losing control of our individual and collective futures. Relatively simple algorithmic systems already steer human decision-making, such as social media feed algorithms that lead people to unintentionally and absent-mindedly scroll through engagement-optimized content. In this paper, we develop the idea of human agency by integrating philosophical and scientific theories of agency with AI-assisted evaluation methods: using large language models (LLMs) to simulate and validate user queries and to evaluate AI responses. We develop HumanAgencyBench (HAB), a scalable and adaptive diagnostic tool for six behaviors related to human agency. HAB measures the tendency of an AI assistant to Ask Clarifying Questions, Avoid Value Manipulation, Correct Misinformation, Defer Important Decisions, Encourage Learning, and Maintain Social Boundaries. We find low-to-moderate agency support in contemporary LLM-based assistants, with substantial variation across system developers and behaviors. For example, while Anthropic LLMs most support human agency overall, they are the least supportive LLMs in terms of Avoid Value Manipulation. These behaviors do not appear to consistently result from increasing LLM capabilities or instruction-following (e.g., RLHF); we encourage further study of these behaviors so that developers and users can better understand the complexities of modern human-AI interaction.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Structured World-State Reasoning for Agentic Robotic Search
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Finley R. Holt, Luis A. Pabon, John Irvin Alora, Jonas Frey, Marco Pavone
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: WORLDS is a novel framework for robotic search that effectively integrates natural language processing, geospatial priors, and real-time observations, achieving the highest navigation success rate to date.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Long-horizon robotic search must resolve natural language against heterogeneous, incomplete, and often ambiguous evidence: textual information, prior maps, and observations arriving over time. The core challenge is to contextualize these streams and decide where to gather evidence before selecting a target. We present WORLDS: World-state Observation and Reasoning for Language-guided Discovery and Search, a framework that grounds reasoning in a persistent graph initialized from geospatial priors and updated by perception. Parallel Reasoners maintain competing candidate interpretations and request evidence to distinguish between them. We collect and process the requested observations with a multimodal Examiner, after which a Judge selects a grounded target or requests another pass. WORLDS achieves 51.8% navigation success across all 5,311 CityNav test episodes, the highest reported success rate, exceeding the previous published best by 15.7 percentage points under an OSM-only, high-resolution orthographic protocol. On 1,000 shared episodes, it achieves 50.0% versus 27.9% for the strongest adapted baseline using the same model, prior, sensing stack, and movement budget. Observation-based verification by the Examiner contributes 5.9 points of this success, and at a reduced reasoning-effort setting WORLDS still exceeds the adapted GeoNav baseline by 18.8 points while generating fewer tokens. We also demonstrate WORLDS on a quadrotor, which flies the generated sensing waypoints and grounds three language targets, including a vehicle absent from the map, from its onboard imagery.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Observing and Controlling Features in Vision-Language-Action Models
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Hugo Buurmeijer, Carmen Amo Alonso, Aiden Swann, Marco Pavone
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper explores lightweight behavioral steering in Vision-Language-Action models using linear observers and controllers, enhancing output alignment without retraining and with minimal overhead.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown remarkable progress towards embodied intelligence. While their architecture partially resembles that of Large Language Models (LLMs), VLAs exhibit higher complexity due to their multi-modal inputs/outputs and often hybrid nature of transformer and diffusion heads. This is part of the reason why insights from mechanistic interpretability in LLMs, which explain how the internal model representations relate to their output behavior, do not trivially transfer to VLA counterparts. In this work, we investigate whether VLA internal representations support lightweight behavioral steering without retraining. Across four frontier VLA models, linear \emph{observers} recover state- and action-relevant information in both autoregressive and transformer--flow-matching architectures, and provide robust directions to causally alter VLA outputs. Building on this, we introduce a \emph{controller} that minimally modifies representations to place observer predictions within prescribed target intervals. Closed-loop experiments with $π_{0.5}$ in the LIBERO simulator and on DROID hardware demonstrate improved constraint satisfaction while retaining task performance, with only approximately $1\%$ inference overhead. Together, these experiments show that lightweight linear interventions can reliably steer VLA behavior while preserving closed-loop capabilities, enabling alignment with user preferences and task requirements without fine-tuning.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Peng Xia, Rujun Han, Zifeng Wang, Yanfei Chen, Yufan Zhang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The RRSI method enhances agent harnesses by incorporating regularization to prevent overfitting during recursive self-improvement, achieving significant performance gains across various benchmarks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: An LLM agent's capability is largely magnified by its harness, namely the prompts, control flow, tooling, memory, and context management surrounding the frozen backbone model. Recent methods increasingly automate this process by iteratively proposing and selecting component-wise edits of an agent harness, practically establishing a form of recursive self-improvement (RSI) at the agent-system level. However, such recursive evolution may overfit by memorizing the training tasks, showing large in-distribution gains that shrink or even vanish on out-of-distribution benchmarks. We introduce Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses (RRSI), which incorporates the principles of regularizations into harness self-improvement by constraining the evolution candidate proposal and selection. The proposer operates with a temporally annealed budget, limiting how many edits a candidate can bundle, and it encourages unexplored trajectories based on evolution history. The selector is equipped with a critic and a pruner: the critic screens benchmark-specific proposals, while the pruner, removes changes that are too small, too expensive, or no longer useful. Together these constraints favor reusable agent mechanisms over benchmark-specific ones or even noises. Across eight benchmarks spanning coding, agentic workspace and engineering design tasks, RRSI gains up to 14.1 points on the split it evolves against and up to 4.7 points on the five out-of-distribution benchmarks, while producing a harness that runs on 30% fewer policy tokens than the unregularized evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/google-research/rrsi and project page is https://regularized-rsi.com/.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: VideoGen-Agent: Reinforcing Video Generation Agents
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Binxu Li, Haoyi Duan, Yuhui Zhang, Yaohui Zhang, Zihao Lin
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: VideoGen-Agent enhances video generation by employing multitask reinforcement learning to effectively utilize external tools, achieving significant improvements in prompt-specific video quality and consistency.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Recent advances in video generative models have enabled high-fidelity, temporally coherent video generation. However, these models often struggle to satisfy prompts requiring specialized knowledge, specific identities, physical consistency, or ordered events. In this paper, we present VideoGen-Agent, a multimodal agent trained through multitask agentic reinforcement learning to use external tools for video generation. The agent coordinates augmentation, generation, and verification tools through multi-turn interactions, using the prompt and intermediate observations to guide its decisions. We train a shared policy on a category-balanced dataset spanning six tasks. Supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated trajectories establishes tool-use behavior, which is then refined through reinforcement learning. A category-aware hybrid reward evaluates tool-call validity, task-appropriate tool use, and generated video quality. We further introduce VABench, a held-out benchmark of 600 prompts covering procedural knowledge, single- and multi-entity identity preservation, physical consistency, scene composition, and multi-shot temporal structure. On VABench, VideoGen-Agent improves over its base text-to-video generator by 19.1 points, from 56.5 to 75.6. Upgrading the generation tools further raises the score to 86.1 without additional agent training. Human raters prefer the upgraded configuration over the strongest standalone baseline in 84.3% of comparisons. These results support learning tool use across video-generation tasks and show that the trained agent can benefit from subsequent advances in generation tools.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Adibvafa Fallahpour, Parsa Idehpour, Vignesh Kothapalli, Nikita Mounier, Shirley Wu
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: Memorilla enhances frozen LLMs by efficiently encoding and retrieving query-specific information from extensive document collections using a limited number of memory tokens, improving performance in various tasks.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent 'memory tokens' for a frozen LLM. Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM's input embedding space. Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering. Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108x fewer tokens to represent the source documents. Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent's past turns) increases throughout the trajectory. In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent's tendency to wander between rooms it has already explored, and improves its average success rate from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. Overall, Memorilla aids frozen LLMs in accumulating and using knowledge effectively across long-context interactions and takes a step towards building continually learning AI systems.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: World Modeling through Spectral Alignment
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Holger Molin, William Peng, Marco Bagatella, Randall Balestriero
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper introduces SpecWM, a framework for world modeling that uses spectral representation learning to enhance latent space control and improve planning success through targeted similarity kernels.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: How do we tell a world model what information to preserve? We study this question through the lens of spectral representation learning. We introduce SpecWM, a JEPA framework that explicitly specifies desired relationships between observations through a target similarity kernel and trains the encoder to reproduce those relationships in its embedding geometry. Different kernels provide different supervision, ranging from physical state information to a fully self-supervised temporal kernel requiring only the ordering of observations within trajectories. We characterize the global optima of the objective, establish conditions for linear recoverability and invariance to nuisance information, and connect temporal-kernel similarity to the behavioral successor measure under an idealized setting. Empirically, the choice of kernel strongly controls which physical quantities are recoverable from the representation. More importantly, temporal spectral alignment improves CEM planning success over LeWorldModel from 52% to 68% on OGBench Cube, 49% to 77% on OGBench Scene, and 29% to 51% on CALVIN. These results suggest that explicitly specifying representation geometry provides a simple way to steer what latent world models preserve for control.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Causal Analysis of Robot Foundation Models Enables Efficiency Gains
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Mozes Jacobs, Siddharth Boppana, Tal Haklay
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper analyzes causal pathways in vision-language-action models, revealing efficiency gains by optimizing action expert conditioning, reducing inference costs without sacrificing performance.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising approach to general purpose robot manipulation. While the internal computation of vision-language models, which compose the backbone of VLAs, has been studied extensively, less is known about how their perceptual and semantic representations are transformed into action in VLA models. We study this question mechanistically in three frontier VLA models ($π_{0.5}$, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot) by analyzing the causal pathways through which the input image and the instruction shape actions. Across the three models, activation patching shows that causally relevant information influences the action expert (AE) through a narrow band of mid-to-late cross-attention layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface. The content of this information changes with token and layer within the model. Early-to-mid layer representations of the target noun token determine which object is selected, whereas mid-to-late layers carry the spatial information in text tokens that redirects the movement when patched. Where spatial information is stored in prompt tokens various based on the architecture. In MolmoAct2 the model forms task-conditioned representations at the text positions that follow the instruction, whereas $π_{0.5}$ additionally stores this information at image token positions. We show that these findings can be translated directly into improving model efficiency. We find that restricting MolmoBot's action expert conditioning to only 3 out of 36 layers reduces inference FLOPs by up to $33\%$ while maintaining comparable task success with the default model across 3,000 evaluation episodes ($46.7\%$ vs. $46.9\%$), and the same principle carries over to real-robot deployment of $π_{0.5}$.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Multi-Dimensional Featurizers Yield Fine-Grained Steering and Data Shaping in Robot Foundation Models
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Aiden Swann, Mozes Jacobs, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, David Chanin
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper demonstrates that block-sparse featurizers enhance robot behavior control by enabling interpretable steering and data shaping through multi-dimensional feature recovery.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn. We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model's computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than $1.4\%$ of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Play2Perfect: What Matters in Dexterous Play Pretraining for Precise Assembly?
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Tyler Ga Wei Lum, Kushal Kedia, C. Karen Liu, Jeannette Bohg
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The Play2Perfect framework enhances robotic assembly by pretraining through diverse play, achieving significant efficiency and success in precise manipulation tasks.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Multi-fingered robots promise the speed and dexterity of human hands, yet challenging problems such as precise assembly have remained out of reach. These tasks are contact-rich, making data collection for imitation learning difficult, and sparse-reward, making direct exploration with reinforcement learning (RL) intractable. Consequently, prior work has made progress by structuring the problem with specialized grippers, tool attachments, and environment fixtures. In this work, we argue that before a robot can perfect precise assembly, it must first learn to play. We further ask the question: what factors in the process of learning to play matter for precise assembly? We propose Play2Perfect, an RL framework for task-agnostic pretraining through play on diverse objects and goals, which is then perfected on precise assembly. The goal of play is to acquire reusable manipulation priors, such as grasping, in-hand reorientation and pose reaching. Finetuning then adapts this general prior to assembly, focusing exploration on the final contact-rich, high-precision interactions needed for success. We systematically study key design choices in play pretraining, including object diversity, training objective, trajectory diversity, and goal precision. We show that our prior is 33x more sample-efficient than RL training from scratch, even when provided with dense, multi-stage rewards. We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, achieving 60% success on tight insertions with only 0.5 mm contact clearance, and over 50% success on long-horizon multi-part assembly and screwing.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Bridging the Markerless Tracking Validation Gap: Intraoperative X-ray Workflow Integration
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Connor Daly, Salvatore Russo, Jinendra Ekanayake, Daniel S. Elson, Ferdinando Rodriguez y Baena
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper presents a novel pipeline integrating intraoperative X-ray with RGB-D sensors for accurate validation of markerless spinal tracking, establishing a reliable ground truth for clinical applications.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Markerless intraoperative tracking of spinal anatomy via RGB-D sensors is a promising alternative to invasive bone-anchored fiducials, yet no existing clinical dataset provides independent subsurface ground truth for validating these methods. We address this gap with a clinically viable pipeline that derives per-vertebra 6-DoF pose from routine intraoperative C-arm fluoroscopy, co-registered to the RGB-D camera frame through a multimodal fiducial array detectable in both imaging modalities. Critically, the pipeline requires no additional radiation, instrumentation, or deviation from standard surgical workflows, relying solely on the fluoroscopic images already acquired during routine level checks. A calibrated transform chain links the vertebral pose recovered via multi-view 2D-3D CT-to-fluoroscopy registration to the RGB-D coordinate frame, enabling direct comparison of any markerless registration estimate against a subsurface reference. Ex vivo validation against optically tracked ovine vertebrae confirms end-to-end accuracy of 2.06 +- 0.29 mm and 3.35 +- 0.93 degrees, sufficient to serve as independent ground truth for methods with substantially larger errors. We demonstrate the pipeline's utility by evaluating two markerless registration strategies on clinical data spanning 11 vertebrae across 1,500 frames from three surgical sequences: the first such evaluation against an independent subsurface reference in a clinical setting. The proposed framework provides reusable infrastructure for benchmarking emerging markerless tracking methods on real surgical data.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Safe and Fuel-Efficient Motion Planning for Lunar Propulsive Drones
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Elena Wittemyer, Graco Gao
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper presents an autonomous motion planning framework for lunar drones that ensures safe, fuel-efficient hops using vision-guided control and obstacle detection.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Propulsive drones are a promising new technology for generating high-resolution terrain models of the Moon. In future lunar missions, propulsive drones will complete a series of hops across the lunar surface while capturing images with downward-facing cameras. We present an autonomous motion planning framework that uses a vision-guided optimal control strategy for performing safe, efficient hops between specified waypoints. The drone plans parabolic hops between waypoints generated by a global-level planner; if a nominal waypoint is unsafe or unreachable, the drone then completes a diversion maneuver to safely land. To evaluate the validity of potential landing sites, we develop a custom semantic segmentation model for identifying obstacles from aerial images, and we introduce an approach for rapidly calculating reachable terrain. We then use model predictive control (MPC) to robustly track hop trajectories that guide the drone towards safe landing sites. We test the optimal hop planner in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. Our results demonstrate that our unified motion planning framework yields safe, fuel-efficient hop trajectories which can be tracked rapidly and with low error via MPC.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Anikait Singh, Teresa Zhang, Yoonho Lee, Roshen Sanjay Nair, Aviral Kumar
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: Librarian Agents enhance LLMs by proactively organizing unstructured data into tailored workspaces, improving query response accuracy and efficiency through reinforcement learning.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Chenyuan Zhou, Yining Hong, Huang Huang, Yunfan Jiang, Wenlong Huang
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: T2-Z optimizes environment latents at test time, enhancing robotic world models to improve predictions and action success in diverse settings without prior environmental knowledge.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Mozes Jacobs, Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, Fenil R. Doshi
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper explores the multi-dimensional geometric representations of task-relevant concepts in vision-language-action models, revealing their significance in robotic manipulation beyond mere readability.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: The Invisible Leash: Why RLVR May or May Not Escape Its Origin
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Fang Wu, Weihao Xuan, Danny Xing, Ximing Lu, Mingjie Liu
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper critiques Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), revealing it may enhance reliability of known outputs while limiting access to diverse verified solutions.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Recent advances highlight Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) as a promising approach to enhancing LLM capabilities. However, it remains unclear whether the current practice of RLVR truly expands models' reasoning boundary or mainly amplifies high-reward outputs that base models already know. We introduce empirical support dynamics, a framework that quantifies how RLVR preserves, expands, and shrinks access to verified solutions. Applied across models, reasoning tasks, and training checkpoints, it matches verified successes question by question to reveal changes that aggregate accuracy can conceal. Across the evaluated model-level benchmark aggregates, \textit{the shrinkage of observed support outweighs its expansion}: more questions lose a verified success than gain one at the stated sampling budgets. These losses occur alongside gains in \texttt{pass@1}. Some RLVR models increase average token-level entropy while reducing final-answer entropy: their token choices become more uncertain on average even as their final answers become more concentrated. Together, these findings reveal an ``invisible leash'' in current RLVR practice: it can make existing successes more reliable while losing access to other verified solutions. Empirical support dynamics make this imbalance measurable and motivate exploration strategies that reach underrepresented solutions while retaining prior successes.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Constrained Whole-Body Tracking for Humanoid Robots
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Daniel Morton, Pranit Mohnot, Marco Pavone
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper presents ConstrainedMimic, a control framework that ensures real-time constraint enforcement in humanoid robot motion tracking using reinforcement learning, enhancing safety and agility.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have demonstrated impressive whole-body agility for humanoid robots, yet ensuring safety and satisfying constraints -- particularly those specified after training -- remains a challenge. Towards this goal, we present ConstrainedMimic, a control framework that leverages whole-body kinematics and dynamics for real-time constraint enforcement within RL tracking policies. By integrating principles from operational space control and control barrier functions, we enable the satisfaction of arbitrary runtime constraints on both the kinematic reference motion and the underlying dynamics, with efficient computation at frequencies above 1 kHz. In whole-body motion-tracking experiments in simulation and hardware, we demonstrate collision avoidance (both with the robot body and external obstacles), joint limits, and center of mass stability constraints. By remaining consistent with the current contact mode and tracking objectives, we minimally restrict the capabilities of the policy when constraints are active. Project page: https://stanfordasl.github.io/constrainedmimic.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: LEGS: Fine-Tuning Teleop-Free VLAs for Humanoid Loco-manipulation in an Embodied Gaussian Splatting World
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Hojune Kim, Timothy Chen, Jiankai Sun, Lars W. Osterberg, Qianzhong Chen
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: LEGS introduces a hybrid simulator for humanoid loco-manipulation, enabling scalable, teleoperation-free training of vision-language-action policies that outperform traditional methods.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies for humanoid loco-manipulation is constrained by the high cost and complexity of collecting human teleoperation demonstrations. VLA policies fine-tuned in simulators have so far transferred poorly to humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. We present LEGS (Loco-manipulation via Embodied Gaussian Splatting), a hybrid simulator that composites a mesh foreground (robot, objects, props) over a photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) background reconstructed from a handheld scene capture. LEGS uses a procedural motion-primitive generator to synthesize labeled demonstrations at scale without human teleoperation, and a two-stage color calibration that aligns renders to the deployment camera. On a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, across three pick-and-place tasks of increasing whole-body difficulty and three VLA backbones ($ψ_0$, $π_{0.5}$, GR00T N1.6), a policy trained purely on LEGS data matches or exceeds one trained on human teleoperation demos on every experiment. It also outperforms a mesh-only baseline trained on the same motions without the calibrated 3DGS frontend. Because motion is recorded independently of appearance, the same demonstrations can be re-rendered for a target scene and objects at over 15x lower cost than teleoperation. When both the objects and the scene change, a policy trained on LEGS-AUG data re-rendered for that target maintains task success, while the teleop baseline fails entirely. Code and videos are available at https://hojjunekim.github.io/legs/.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Jadelynn Dao, Milan Ganai, Yasmina Abukhadra, Ajay Sridhar, Mozhgan Nasr Azadani
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The DIRECT framework optimizes test-time compute allocation in embodied planners, enhancing performance while reducing latency and resource usage compared to traditional scaling methods.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as high-level planners for embodied agents, with an emerging strategy of scaling test-time compute to improve capability. However, we observe that doing so increases latency, token usage, and FLOPs while yielding uneven, often diminishing gains in downstream success, limiting where embodied agents can be deployed. We argue that choosing when and where to spend test-time compute is central to bringing frontier performance to the real world, and we can budget inference at the planning level. We introduce DIRECT, a routing framework that uses multimodal scene context to allocate compute at each step of a closed-loop agent, selecting a planner for every subtask, improving the success--cost Pareto frontier over fixed model selection. Across three dominant scaling axes, namely chain-of-thought depth, model size, and memory history, our experiments on VLABench and RoboMME show that test-time compute is not a uniform lever: different axes yield qualitatively distinct capability gains. We validate these insights on a physical Franka arm in a DROID setup spanning zero-shot manipulation and long-horizon chaining, where our router matches or exceeds a stronger model's success rate at up to 65% lower average latency. Ultimately, our results show that naively scaling test-time compute is wasteful, and DIRECT can provide frontier-level embodied planning at a fraction of the cost. Project page can be found at jadee-dao.github.io/direct/.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: TrAct: Bridging Robot Control and Visual Prediction with Visual Tracks
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Zhi Cao, Howard Ji, Kevin Zhang, Kuangzhi Ge, Li Fei-Fei
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: TrAct enhances robot decision-making by using visual tracks as an embodiment-agnostic interface, improving action prediction and task success rates in simulations and real-world scenarios.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Robot actions are inherently embodiment-specific and only weakly aligned with image-space visual changes, limiting their effectiveness as conditioning signals for robot world models. In contrast, visual tracks provide an embodiment-agnostic representation of how task-relevant points move through a scene, offering dense image-space guidance for accurate and spatially precise future video prediction. Building on this observation, we propose TrAct, a world-model-based robot decision-making framework that uses visual tracks as an intermediate interface between control and prediction. TrAct consists of three components: a Vision-Language-Action-and-Track model (VLAT) that jointly predicts candidate actions and corresponding visual tracks from the current observation and language instruction; a track-conditioned world model (TWM) that predicts future visual outcomes conditioned on the proposed tracks; and a vision-language reward model (VLAC) that scores the predicted outcomes. At inference time, VLAT generates candidate action-track pairs, TWM rolls out their visual consequences, and VLAC selects the track whose predicted outcome best satisfies the instruction; the action paired with the selected track is then executed by the robot. Experiments on the proposed LIBERO-INTEGRAL benchmark and real-world Franka manipulation show that TrAct improves success rates from 27% to 55% in simulation and from 49% to 76% on real-world tasks compared with the strong VLA baseline $π_{0.5}$. Furthermore, TWM consistently improves video prediction quality over the action-conditioned world model (AWM). These results demonstrate that visual tracks provide an effective shared interface between robot control and visual prediction, enabling more accurate world modeling and stronger robot generalization.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: FACT: A Multimodal Force-Action-Track Foundation Model for Human-to-Robot Dexterity
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Zhi Cao, Yining Hong, Jiaolong Yang, Yejin Choi, Li Fei-Fei
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The FACT model integrates a large-scale human tactile dataset with robot demonstrations to enhance dexterous manipulation through force-aware planning and refinement, achieving significant performance improvements.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative to costly robot data collection for dexterous manipulation, but most human datasets lack force measurements. Dexterous manipulation requires not only visual and proprioceptive understanding but also the ability to anticipate and regulate interaction forces. To scale force-aware human-robot co-training, we introduce EgoForce, a large-scale human tactile dataset capturing force-rich manipulation experience, and combine it with robot demonstrations for pretraining. We present FACT, a robot foundation model that cascades from prospective visual planning to force-aware refinement for dexterous manipulation. FACT comprises two jointly trained components. A Track-Guided Coarse Planner jointly predicts actions, future video, and visual tracks. Future video and visual tracks also provide a shared task representation that facilitates cross-embodiment knowledge transfer and coarse action generation. Building on this coarse plan, a Force-Action Joint Refiner jointly predicts future force and refines the coarse action, allowing anticipated force and action to shape each other during refinement. We evaluate the model on ten tasks requiring fine-grained coordination and force feedback, including tool use, musical instruments, and precision laboratory procedures. Using as few as 10 robot trajectories with 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning, FACT outperforms both baselines, with success-rate gains of up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex. Ablations show that force supervision in human pretraining data is crucial for downstream robot performance after fine-tuning, while visual track prediction and training with future-force prediction improve dexterous execution. Experiments varying the human-robot data ratio during fine-tuning further suggest that FACT learns from human demonstrations nearly as effectively as from robot demonstrations.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: End-to-End Vision-Language-Action Policies for Autonomous Lunar Rover Docking
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Sitan Huang, Grace Gao
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper presents an end-to-end vision-language-action policy for lunar rover docking, demonstrating competitive performance against modular navigation under perceptual disturbances with adaptive execution for safety.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Surface navigation on the Moon is subject to extreme illumination contrast and deployment-time perceptual disturbances. While modular navigation pipelines have long supported planetary rover navigation, robustness is compromised by measurement errors that propagate through hand-engineered components. End-to-end learned policies are an alternative approach to navigation, which maps observations directly to control actions without intermediate components. Vision-language-action models, in particular, have driven significant breakthroughs in robotics and autonomous vehicle research. By leveraging internet-scale vision-language pretraining, these models can be exploited for their commonsense reasoning and visual understanding to provide robust generalization with limited task-specific data. However, their applicability and performance have yet to be characterized for lunar surface operations. In this study, we design a vision-language-action policy for autonomous lunar rover docking and characterize its performance relative to a modular navigation pipeline. We develop a scalable training framework that generates safety-aware expert demonstrations in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. In closed-loop evaluations, our policy performs competitively relative to the modular baseline under perceptual disturbances unseen during training. To address the tradeoff between compute consumption and closed-loop safety, the policy adapts its execution horizon by determining how far the rover may safely travel in open loop. Adaptive-horizon execution reduces inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates relative to fixed horizons in the evaluated scenarios.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Full-Order Safety for Nonlinear Reduced-Order MPC
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Luis Pabon, Johannes Köhler, Revant Kasichainula, Marco Pavone
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: CoRE-MPC ensures safety and efficiency in nonlinear model predictive control by using robust reduced-order models, maintaining constraint satisfaction while significantly reducing computational demands.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Reduced-order models (ROMs) make model predictive control (MPC) of high-dimensional nonlinear systems tractable, but the resulting modeling error can lead to constraint violations on the real system. We introduce CoRE-MPC, a robust MPC formulation that plans with a nonlinear ROM and guarantees recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction for the full-order system. It can be applied with a broad class of nonlinear model reduction techniques and the resulting MPC does not require evaluating the full-order model online, thus ensuring computational efficiency. The key insight is in how the ROM affects the dynamics of the prediction error. We account for this with two error radii that are propagated alongside the ROM and provide a guaranteed bound on the prediction error. The approach is validated in simulation on an 80-state oscillator chain, a Burgers equation, and a 9,768-state finite-element soft robot, where a two-state ROM with data-driven bounds keeps all 1,628 nodes clear of a wall at a median solve time below 1 ms for a 20 ms control period. Across these examples, CoRE-MPC is 13 to 61 times faster than full-order robust MPC at only 27 to 35% higher closed-loop cost, whereas existing certified schemes are either infeasible or at least twice as conservative. Code: [released upon publication].

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Back on Track: Deployment-time Policy Improvement via World Model Planning
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Colton Crosby, Hao Wang, Mac Schwager, Somil Bansal
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper presents a framework that enhances visuomotor policy performance during deployment by using a world model for real-time monitoring and corrective planning.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice. We instead propose an offline-trained monitoring-and-intervention framework that improves a policy during deployment using only black-box query access. From a limited set of labeled on-policy rollouts, we learn a policy-conditioned liveness value that measures the nominal policy's progress toward task completion; we additionally train a compact latent world model using these rollouts together with play data. At deployment, the liveness value continuously monitors execution. When it detects a loss of progress, a short-horizon planner searches the world model for corrective actions using the same value as its planning objective, after which control returns to the nominal policy. We evaluate our method on the LIBERO-Goal task suite and on a Franka Panda manipulator, using the vision-language-action model $π_{0.5}$ and a diffusion policy as nominal policies, and demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, while supporting real-time control. Additional results and videos are available on the project website (https://policy-improvement-wm.pages.dev/).

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Efficient Noise Context-Aware Representation for Low-Dose CT Denoising
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Minwoo Yu, N. Robert Bennett, Jongduk Baek, Adam S. Wang
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The ENCORE framework enhances low-dose CT denoising by leveraging specific noise characteristics and anatomical features, improving quality and efficiency through adaptive convolution and zero-shot conditional denoising.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: While deep learning-based denoising has become widely adopted in low-dose CT, conventional models use generic architectures designed for natural images, failing to account for non-stationary and spatially correlated CT noise characteristics. To address this, we propose an Efficient Noise COntext-aware REpresentation (ENCORE) framework that explicitly leverages CT noise characteristics and anatomical features. First, we reformulate the noise synthesis procedure based on a realistic noise distribution beyond the conventional Gaussian approximation, establishing a rigorous foundation for training pair generation. Next, we extract local noise power and correlation contexts to guide the denoising process. To fully leverage the potential of noise context, we propose a FlyingConv module, which adaptively changes convolution weights for each local image region. Notably, our approach demonstrates substantial gains in both denoising quality and computational efficiency. Furthermore, manipulating the intensity of the noise context maps at inference time enables zero-shot conditional denoising, allowing for dynamic control over the output image texture. The entire pipeline is available at https://github.com/minwoo-yu/ENCORE.git

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: FoveaVLA: Foveation Actions Replace the Wrist Camera in VLAs
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Bingao Chen, Lihan Zha, C. Karen Liu, Guy Tevet
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: FoveaVLA enhances Vision-Language-Action models by using learned foveation actions to replace wrist cameras, improving manipulation success rates in complex tasks.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost. FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on $π_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $π_{0.5}$. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Kaifei Wang, Zikang Shan, Liwei Wang, Yinyu Ye, Han Zhong
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper investigates the role of bias-corrected exponential moving average momentum in reinforcement learning, demonstrating that optimal momentum selection enhances performance in policy gradient optimization.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $β$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $β$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $η$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $β$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $β$ to keep $η/(1-β)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $β_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: PanTact: Teaching Whole-Body Dexterity with a Wearable Contact Interface
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Xiaomeng Xu, Han Zhang, Zhian Ruan, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: PanTact enables humanoid robots to learn whole-body dexterity through a wearable interface that captures human demonstrations, facilitating manipulation beyond hand-centric approaches.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Humanoid robots have many degrees of freedom and contact surfaces, yet most loco-manipulation research restricts manipulation to the hands and avoids other body contacts with the environment. To extend manipulation beyond the hands, we present PanTact, a system that learns humanoid whole-body dexterity, the capability to manipulate with any suitable body surface, directly from robot-free human demonstrations. Our key idea is to use contact as manipulation-centric information that transfers across embodiments. Contact locations and timing specify the interactions needed to accomplish a task, while the robot chooses how to coordinate its body to realize them within its own physical constraints. Specifically, PanTact captures, learns, and executes whole-body contact via: 1) a wearable, robot-free data collection interface that augments egocentric vision and bimanual UMI grippers with whole-body modular contact patches to record body contact locations and states; 2) a visuomotor policy that mitigates the egocentric observation gap and predicts whole-body contact goals; and 3) contact-aware whole-body control formulations that realize active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces. We deploy PanTact on a Unitree G1 humanoid without additional body contact sensors, demonstrating whole-body dexterity involving body support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing. Website: https://pantact.github.io

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Ximing Lu, Aviral Kumar, Jan Kautz, Yejin Choi, David Acuna
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: MagicBeanStalk introduces a recursive data-synthesis algorithm that effectively generates calibrated training problems for RLVR, significantly improving model performance across various benchmarks.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Data-centric scaling of RLVR has focused on collecting or generating verifiable training problems. However, corpus size alone does not determine whether the dataset provides a useful learning signal for a target policy. To guide the synthesis of effective RLVR data, we experimentally characterize dataset effectiveness as a function of its problems, the target policy, and the training rollout budget. Under this characterization, we show that a large open-source math corpus pooled from widely used RLVR datasets falls almost entirely into a zero-advantage trap: for a fixed target policy and rollout budget, roughly 88% of its problems are solved in every rollout or failed in every rollout. Filtering concentrates what remains, but it can only select, discarding the hard problems. Effective synthetic problems should therefore require the reasoning operations and compositions required to solve those hard problems. Yet their difficulty must be calibrated, so that some rollouts succeed, some fail, and at least one correct solution fits within the training budget. Prompting a teacher to vary hard problems directly does not achieve this. Guided by these empirical principles, we introduce MagicBeanStalk, a top-down decomposition and bottom-up recursive data-synthesis algorithm that grows seed problems into families of substantively new, policy- and budget-calibrated training problems while preserving the seeds' reasoning blueprints. Across 8 math benchmarks, continual RLVR on MagicBeanStalk problems improves gpt-oss-120b from 61.2 to 69.8 (+8.6) and DeepSeek v4Flash from 72.4 to 77.9 (+5.4) on a 16K-token budget. Training on the full 78K source corpus improves by only +1.1 and its best filtered real data subset by +5.8. In finance, we synthesize over 14K verifiable problems from only 340 solutions and improve over base by 6.9 and 2.4 points on SecQue and FinanceBench, respectively.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: FallGown: A Soft Pneumatic Wearable Device for Fall Prevention
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Megan C. Coram, Haoran Lei, Steven H. Collins, Steve B. Cousins, Michelle Baldonado
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The FallGown is a lightweight, soft pneumatic wearable device designed to prevent falls in older adults, offering support while enabling mobility and monitored exercise.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Concerns about falling and potential resulting injuries prevent many older adults from participating in forms of health-improving exercise such as walking, dance, and tai chi. Existing passive devices like walkers require use of the arms for support, and active devices like exoskeletons and robotic frames are often rigid, bulky, and stigmatized, which limits their use. The FallGown is a soft wearable support structure consisting of pressurized pneumatic pouches within a fabric shell; it can support the full weight of a user's body and aims to prevent falls. It is portable (6.9 kg and 0.051 m3 when stored), minimally burdensome (7.24-20.8 N drag force depending on floor type and whether an optional rolling base frame is used), and convenient (less than 2.5 minutes on average to don and less than 0.5 minutes on average to doff). The optional rolling base lowers friction with the floor, but reduces portability and skirt deformation (which can be useful to fit through doors and other tight spaces). Fall prevention testing with a single user revealed a tradeoff between device size and stability against tipping; a skirt with 12 pneumatic pouches and a floor diameter of 1.4 meters with a base frame prevented all falls except in one case with a mechanical failure. On-board pressure sensors can sense the user's weight distribution, providing an opportunity for monitored exercise and adaptive support.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Taoyang Jia, Weikai Huang, Linxin Song, Jared Darlington, Jieyu Zhao
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: Reflex is a novel framework enabling humanoid robots to catch thrown boxes by integrating whole-body control, real-time object dynamics inference, and egocentric visual perception.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision. We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable. In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers' success at the same distances.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: BT-Agent: Deploying Onboard Robot Agents with Behavior Trees and Multi-Fidelity Evaluation
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Fabio Hübel, Adam Lilja, Yue Yin, Siming He, Claire Tomlin
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: BT-Agent integrates LLM-driven task reasoning with behavior-tree skills for efficient onboard robot operation, demonstrating improved performance and evaluation through a novel multi-fidelity benchmark.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Deploying language-model agents onboard mobile robots requires task reasoning and responsive execution within limited compute and memory. We propose BT-Agent, an onboard architecture combining LLM-driven task decisions with predefined behavior-tree (BT) skills. These skills enforce execution conditions and return structured failure feedback. We demonstrate fully onboard operation with a 9B model on a quadruped across five task categories. Intervention tests show that local checks stop ongoing navigation without waiting for another model decision, while the agent remains active to retry or report constraints. To compare agent designs efficiently, we introduce a 161-task multi-fidelity benchmark, evaluated in text on all tasks and in Habitat on 39. Text supports 10.9$\times$ higher evaluation throughput, while simulation reveals how perception and motion failures change task outcomes. BT-Agent's largest success gains over the strongest Act/ReAct baseline occur at 4B and 9B: approximately 10 and 5 percentage points. Ablations identify structured tool calls and informative failure feedback as the most useful components.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Chronos Policy: Learning Robot Policies on Physical Time
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Changhao Wang, Jaden Clark, Shuran Song
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: Chronos Policy enhances robot learning by explicitly incorporating physical time into action sequences, improving performance on dynamic and multisensory tasks while maintaining robustness in quasi-static scenarios.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Robot policies often convert sensing and control into fixed-rate observation-action sequences, leaving physical time implicit in sequence position. This assumption breaks when observation rates or delays vary, or when inference latency changes. We introduce Chronos Policy, which makes physical time explicit by conditioning on observation capture times and desired action execution times. We study two ways to incorporate time into a diffusion transformer: adding timestamp embeddings to token features, or encoding physical time in positional encoding through time-aware rotary positional encodings (time-aware RoPE). We find that time-aware RoPE is more robust, allowing attention to depend directly on physical time while keeping token content unchanged. During training, we temporally randomize which observations are sampled and when the action chunk begins, exposing the policy to a wider range of sensing and execution schedules that may occur during deployments. This also enables learning from asynchronous, multi-rate data without forcing all measurements onto a fixed temporal grid. Across simulation and real-world experiments, Chronos Policy improves performance on dynamic tasks, where observation-to-action timing is critical, and on multisensory tasks, where the relative timing between observations matters. On standard quasi-static tasks, it preserves nominal performance while improving robustness to changes in sensing and inference timing.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Mayank Mittal, Fan Yang, Alexander Hansson
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: DeFM is a self-supervised foundation model for depth images that enhances robotic task performance and generalization through geometric and semantic representation learning.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Depth sensors are widely deployed across robotic platforms, and advances in fast, high-fidelity depth simulation have enabled robotic policies trained on depth observations to achieve robust sim-to-real transfer for a wide range of tasks. Despite this, representation learning for depth modality remains underexplored compared to RGB, where large-scale foundation models now define the state of the art. To address this gap, we present DeFM, a self-supervised foundation model trained entirely on depth images for robotic applications. Using a DINO-style self-distillation objective on a curated dataset of 60M depth images, DeFM learns geometric and semantic representations that generalize to diverse environments, tasks, and sensors. To retain metric awareness across multiple scales, we introduce a novel input normalization strategy. We further distill DeFM into compact models suitable for resource-constrained robotic systems. When evaluated on depth-based classification, segmentation, navigation, locomotion, and manipulation benchmarks, DeFM achieves state-of-the-art performance and demonstrates strong generalization from simulation to real-world environments. We release all our pretrained models, which can be adopted off-the-shelf for depth-based robotic learning without task-specific fine-tuning. Webpage: https://de-fm.github.io/

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Injecting Hallucinations in Autonomous Vehicles: A Component-Agnostic Safety Evaluation Framework
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Alexandre Moreira Nascimento, Gabriel Kenji Godoy Shimanuki, Lúcio Flavio Vismari, João Batista Camargo, Jorge Rady de Almeida
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper presents a configurable framework for injecting perception hallucinations in autonomous vehicles, enhancing safety evaluation by quantifying their impact on collision risks in simulations.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Perception failures in autonomous vehicles (AV) remain a major safety concern because they can directly compromise decision-making and contribute to unsafe behavior. To study how these failures affect safety, researchers typically inject artificial faults into real-world or simulated components and observe the resulting outcomes. However, existing fault injection (FI) studies often target a single sensor within the machine perception (MP) module, resulting in siloed frameworks that are difficult to generalize or integrate into unified simulation environments. This work addresses that limitation by reframing perception failures as hallucinations, that is, false perceptions that distort an AV's situational awareness and may trigger unsafe control actions. Building on this concept, we propose a configurable, component-agnostic hallucination injection framework that induces six plausible hallucination types in an open-source simulation environment. A total of 18,356 simulations (8,695 baseline and 9,661 with hallucinations injected) were executed while AVs crossed an unsignalized intersection with transversal traffic. The results statistically validate the framework and quantify the impact of each hallucination type on collisions and on the minimum distance between the AV and the nearest vehicle, used as a continuous proxy for the safety margin. Certain hallucinations, especially missed detection, blind region, angular drift, phantom perception, and latency, significantly increase the odds of collision, while linear drift significantly reduces minimum distances without producing a statistically significant increase in collision odds in the evaluated scenario. The proposed framework provides a scalable and statistically grounded method for evaluating AV safety under perception distortions and supports future research on fault tolerance and resilient AV design.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Infinite-Dimensional Closed-Loop Inverse Kinematics for Soft Robots via Neural Operators
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Carina Veil, Moritz Flaschel, Ellen Kuhl, Cosimo Della Santina
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper presents an infinite-dimensional closed-loop inverse kinematics approach for soft robots, utilizing neural operators to learn actuation-to-shape mappings and derive task-specific control.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: For fully actuated rigid robots, kinematic inversion is a purely geometric problem, efficiently solved by closed-loop inverse kinematics (CLIK) schemes that compute joint velocities to position the robot body in space. For underactuated soft robots, however, not all configurations are attainable through control action, making kinematic inversion extremely ill-posed. Extensions of CLIK address this by introducing end-to-end mappings from actuation to task space for the controller to operate on, but typically assume finite dimensions of the underlying virtual configuration space. In this work, we formulate CLIK in the infinite-dimensional domain to reason about the entire soft robot shape while solving tasks, thereby skipping intermediate approximation steps. We do this by composing an actuation-to-shape map with a shape-to-task map, deriving the differential end-to-end kinematics via an infinite-dimensional chain rule, and thereby obtaining a Jacobian-based CLIK algorithm. Since complex soft-robot models are rarely available in closed form, and neither the actuation-to-shape mapping nor its Jacobian can typically be obtained analytically, we propose to learn it using differentiable neural operator networks. We first present an analytical study on a constant-curvature segment, and then apply the neural version of the algorithm to a three-fiber soft robotic arm whose underlying model relies on morphoelasticity and active filament theory.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Megha Srivastava, Cedric Colas, Dorsa Sadigh, Jacob Andreas
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck framework enhances AI agents' interpretability and generalization by integrating linguistic rule generation with policy learning across diverse tasks.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Modern AI systems such as self-driving cars and game-playing agents can achieve superhuman performance, but often lack human-like generalization, interpretability, and inter-operability with human users. Inspired by the rich interactions between language and decision-making in humans, we introduce Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck (PLLB), a framework enabling AI agents to generate linguistic rules that capture the high-level strategies underlying rewarding behaviors. PLLB alternates between a *rule generation* step guided by language models, and an *update* step where agents learn new policies guided by rules, even when a rule is insufficient to describe an entire complex policy. Across five diverse tasks, including a two-player signaling game, maze navigation, image reconstruction, and robot grasp planning, we show that PLLB agents are not only able to learn more interpretable and generalizable behaviors, but can also share the learned rules with human users, enabling more effective human-AI coordination. We provide source code for our experiments at https://github.com/meghabyte/bottleneck .

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Self-Retrospection Distillation: Turning Post-hoc Experiences into Prior Foresight
