Under the tabular setting, we develop pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for both formulations and establish tight sublinear suboptimality bounds, explicitly capturing how risk sensitivity, encoded by utility functions, affects learning difficulty. Moreover, we establish minimax suboptimality lower bounds to characterize the problem's fundamental limits. To handle large state spaces, we further develop pessimistic least-squares value-iteration algorithms that incorporate the general OCE risk criterion into linear function approximation. We establish utility-dependent sublinear guarantees with explicit dependence on the feature dimension $d$. To our knowledge, we provide the first offline algorithms along with the first upper and lower suboptimality bounds for both dynamic- and static-OCE RL.

OpenDriveLab.title: Dual-Evolving Reinforcement Learning for Automated Reward Design
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Sitao Cheng, Tianle Li, Xuhan Huang, Xunjian Yin, Difan Zou
OpenDriveLab.summary: Dual-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (DERL) enhances automated reward design by using a dual-training framework that adapts reward structures based on inner policy performance feedback.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Crafting effective reward signals remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) for complex reasoning. Existing methods for automated reward optimization search with a fixed proposer which never learns from its costly trials. We present Dual-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (DERL), a dual-training framework for autonomous discovery of reward structures. An outer-loop proposer composes a reward from task primitives, and an inner policy trains with this reward. The proposer itself learns by policy gradient from the validation performance of the inner policy. Thus, DERL utilizes past-trial feedback to shape its reward-proposal distribution, an empirical meta-gradient of task success. We validate DERL on embodied (ALFWorld), scientific (ScienceWorld), and mathematical (GSM8K, MATH) reasoning. On multi-turn agent benchmarks, DERL outperforms strong baselines, significantly on out-of-distribution tasks. In mathematics, DERL improves on the outcome reward where directly added primitives hurt. Further analyses under matched compute show that our proposer effectively captures the meta-gradient to discover useful reward signals.

OpenDriveLab.title: VGGT-Diff: Visual Geometry Meets Diffusion for Sparse-View Novel View Synthesis
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Kangjie Chen, Xiangyu Li, Dongbin Zhang, Chaoda Zheng, Shijia Chen
OpenDriveLab.summary: VGGT-Diff integrates geometry-based routing with a diffusion model for enhanced novel view synthesis from sparse views, achieving state-of-the-art performance through robust conditioning and consistency techniques.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: We present VGGT-Diff, a geometry-routed multi-view diffusion model for sparse-view novel view synthesis. Existing novel view synthesis (NVS) methods face a fundamental trade-off: reconstruction-based approaches preserve observed geometry but struggle to synthesize unseen regions, while diffusion-based methods provide strong generative priors yet rely on implicit source-to-query correspondence. VGGT-Diff bridges these regimes by routing visual geometry latents from VGGT-Ω into a pretrained video diffusion model. Each visual token is associated with a 3D point and confidence, then transformed into query-aligned latent conditions through a confidence-aware Visual Geometry Router (VGR) that preserves front and back surface evidence. These conditions guide joint target-view denoising, while Point-Track Residual Consistency (PTRC) regularizes predicted-clean residuals along reliable 3D tracks, improving multi-view stability. We further introduce robust geometry conditioning, combining training-time regularization with inference-time guidance for improved robustness. Experiments show competitive or state-of-the-art performance across interpolation and extrapolation under different viewpoint difficulties. Our code is available at https://github.com/chenkangjie1123/VGGT-Diff.

OpenDriveLab.title: Coordi-pi: Coordination-Aware Dual-Hand Action Representation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yiming Meng, Yanming Shao, Weijie Shen, Kunyang Lin, Jiayu Sun
OpenDriveLab.summary: Coordi-$\pi$ introduces a structured action representation for bimanual manipulation, enhancing performance significantly by explicitly encoding hand identity and temporal synchronization.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but extending them to bimanual dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional and structured action space. Existing bimanual VLA policies commonly concatenate right- and left-side arm--hand actions at each control timestep, leaving cross-hand interactions implicit within a single action vector. We introduce Coordi-$π$, a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Coordi-$π$ represents the right- and left-side arm--hand actions as individual action tokens and organizes them into an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. To explicitly encode hand identity and temporal synchronization in this interleaved representation, a learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides, while sequence--control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE) separates sequence position from control timestep, allowing actions at the same control timestep to share a temporal coordinate while retaining distinct sequence positions. Across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo, Coordi-$π$ achieves state-of-the-art performance under both \textit{rand-obj} and \textit{rand-full}, improving the average success rate over $π_{0.5}$ from 31.9\% to 51.3\% and from 18.3\% to 32.3\%, respectively. Coordi-$π$ also consistently outperforms $π_{0.5}$ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.

OpenDriveLab.title: LAGO: Language Agents with Reusable Growing Options
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yuran Wu, Mengkang Hu, Qionglin Qiu, Fanqing Meng, Qiguang Chen
OpenDriveLab.summary: LAGO introduces reusable language agents as temporally extended options to enhance task decomposition and execution, achieving improved performance on long-horizon tasks without model weight updates.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Long-horizon tasks expose a weakness of monolithic tool-use loops: one agent must decompose, execute, and verify a task within a single trajectory. We introduce LAGO, which treats specialized language agents as reusable temporally extended options. A meta-agent retrieves options from a persistent library or spawns new ones, dispatches sub-tasks, verifies results, and admits successful novel options. The library grows across tasks without updating model weights. On 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks, frozen Qwen3.5-35B-A3B in both roles resolves 58.6% under single-attempt evaluation with the official Docker evaluator. On a fixed 150-task subset, we re-run mini-SWE-agent, Terminus 2, and LAGO with the same policy, temperature, task IDs, and evaluator; their resolve rates are 49.3%, 57.3%, and 60.3%, respectively. Cross-model experiments provide evidence consistent with a role for decomposition quality. A 50-task component ablation finds four fewer resolved tasks without decomposition, two fewer with shuffled reused content, and six fewer without the library. These results support reusable agent-options as a practical abstraction for task streams, while leaving component-level causality task- and model-dependent.

OpenDriveLab.title: Atomic-WAM: Execution-Grounded Atomic-Motion Reasoning for World Action Models
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Shijun Shi, Zhe Liu, Zhi Hou, Yinan Chen, Tao Zhang
OpenDriveLab.summary: Atomic-WAM integrates task reasoning and action generation through atomic-motion descriptions, enhancing robotic control with execution-grounded learning for improved task success rates.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. Project page: https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic-WAM-project

OpenDriveLab.title: Reflect After Failure: Brain-Inspired Self-Evolving Agents for Embodied Spatial Intelligence
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Xin Li, Xiaohuan Gu, Yifan Wang, Shaobin Ling, Tianli Shi
OpenDriveLab.summary: HiMeco, a brain-inspired self-evolving agent, enhances embodied spatial intelligence by diagnosing failures and refining strategies through metacognitive reflection and memory consolidation.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have made substantial progress in spatial reasoning, and self-evolving agents further extend these capabilities to embodied environments by learning from interactions. However, current self-evolution remains particularly challenging in embodied spatial tasks, complex and multi-step decisions from partial visual evidence making it difficult to determine why an execution fails. The failure may stem from misperception, insufficient exploration, or incorrect planning, yet execution feedback alone rarely reveals which component is responsible. As a result, simply accumulating interaction experience can reinforce ineffective strategies. To address this, we propose HiMeco, a brain-inspired self-evolving agent for embodied spatial intelligence, inspired by metacognitive monitoring and hippocampal memory consolidation. Through Hippocampal-Metacognitive Reflection, HiMeco diagnoses failures in perception-exploration-planning (PEP), then compares execution attempts to derive reusable strategies and guidance for avoiding recurring errors. It also abstracts interaction programs into parameterized skills, using evidence contracts and execution-based validation to determine their retention and reuse. These strategies and skills guide subsequent interactions, with memory updated only between rounds and model parameters kept frozen. HiMeco achieves state-of-the-art performance on ESI-Bench, and it also improves accuracy on EmbSpatial-Bench by 3.94 percentage points without evolution.

OpenDriveLab.title: PingpongDuo: Agile Humanoid Table Tennis Doubles with Safe Team Coordination
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Haoran Jiang, Yichao Zhong, Kai Zhang, Cheng Liu, Yixuan Pan
OpenDriveLab.summary: PingpongDuo is a hierarchical framework enabling agile humanoid table tennis doubles with safe coordination, improving ball-return success by 13.2% and achieving rapid, precise movements.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Unlike singles, humanoid table tennis doubles requires teammates to strike in strict alternation while sharing a confined workspace. Rapid repositioning can compromise striking accuracy, while uncoordinated teammate movements introduce collision risks. We present PingpongDuo, a hierarchical framework for agile humanoid doubles with safe team coordination. At the team level, a planner jointly selects positioning targets and uses learned risk estimates to filter risky proposals, preferentially preserving the current striker's target. At the individual level, separate footwork and striking skills combine agile movement with precise racket control. The skills are guided by human motion references, including footwork collected from human doubles play, and trained from states produced by one another to support rapid transitions. A racket-arm residual further refines strikes after movement using return feedback from a simulator calibrated with real ball-flight and contact measurements. In simulation, PingpongDuo improves the ball-return success rate by 13.2% over the state-of-the-art baseline, while achieving approximately 2 cm positioning error during clearance. In real-world experiments, a robot completes a 2.15 m clearance-and-recovery cycle in 2.4 s with a peak speed of 2.23 m/s, while two robots sustain more than 10 consecutive strikes in strict alternation.

OpenDriveLab.title: REVEAL: Reverse Engineering Agentic Latents from Frontier-Model Traces
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yuetian Du, Meng Wang, Yucheng Wang, Zhangzhe Chen, Wei Wang
OpenDriveLab.summary: The REVEAL framework enables the extraction of reusable local controls from frontier-model trajectories, enhancing smaller agents' performance without requiring model retraining.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Frontier LLM agents perform complex interactive tasks, but their inference costs motivate transferring their experience to smaller open-source agents. Distillation and latent communication typically require target-model training or access to source-model internals. We study how textual frontier-model trajectories can provide reusable local controls for a frozen agent. Inspired by protocol reverse engineering, we introduce $\textit{Agentic Latents}$, comprising anchored states and dynamic profiles of feedback--response cycles elicited by replay in the target model. Our training-free framework, $\textbf{REVEAL}$ ($\textbf{REV}$erse $\textbf{E}$ngineering $\textbf{A}$gentic $\textbf{L}$atents), uses these profiles and trajectory outcomes to match and select local events from successful and failed rollouts of the same task and source model. Their response-transition contrasts yield a target-specific steering direction, applied before each response. Within-benchmark evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Humanity's Last Exam with tools report higher accuracy than unmodified agents across three targets. Representation analyses and behavioral case studies support reusing frontier-model experience as local activation control.

OpenDriveLab.title: DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Dynamics on GPU
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Kemeng Huang, Bowen Ren, Xinyu Lu, Minchen Li, Taku komura
OpenDriveLab.summary: DiffGIPC is a GPU-accelerated framework that efficiently optimizes contact-rich dynamics in deformable and rigid bodies, achieving significant speedups in gradient evaluations while ensuring non-penetration.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Contact-rich inverse problems require efficient gradients and reliable enforcement of non-penetration. Existing differentiable methods provide fast simulation and rigid-deformable coupling, but contact treatments based on penalties or velocity-level constraints can permit penetration or positional drift. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains non-penetration through geometric barriers and {continuous collision detection (CCD)}. However, repeated forward and backward evaluations remain costly in full-space finite-element (FEM) implementations, particularly when nearly rigid components retain many vertex {degrees of freedom (DoFs)}. We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated differentiable IPC framework for optimizing interacting deformable and nearly rigid bodies. Our affine-body derivatives enable {rest-shape} design, initial-state optimization, and articulated control while retaining only twelve motion DoFs per affine body. These gradients account for how changes in geometry, placement, and actuation affect other objects through collision and friction. We preserve these interactions in one coupled FEM-affine adjoint system per frame, reducing the backward-system size without discarding the dependencies that drive the inverse problem. GPU-optimized backward computation further reduces the cost of repeated gradient evaluations. A reusable PyTorch interface connects supported physical parameters to user-defined parameter maps and losses across design, identification, motion, placement, and articulated control. Experiments demonstrate peak speedups over DiffIPC of approximately 150.0x with full-space FEM and 4133.3x with affine bodies for combined forward simulation and backward differentiation.

OpenDriveLab.title: EvoWeave: Composing Reusable Agent Experience through Operation Level Graphs
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Guanhua Zhu, Bo Shen, Lei Zhang, Fadi Deek, Zhi Wei
OpenDriveLab.summary: EvoWeave is a framework that enhances interactive agents' task performance by efficiently composing reusable operations through a structured experience memory and dependency graph.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Different tasks often require interactive agents to perform similar operations at intermediate steps. Retrieving an entire past workflow can introduce irrelevant steps, whereas retrieving isolated operations can discard the dependencies needed to reuse them. We introduce EvoWeave, a framework for experience memory that represents abstract states as nodes and reusable operations as directed edges with input and output contracts, provenance, and capability references. A planner decomposes the current task into a dependency graph; operation retrieval and bounded directed search then assemble relevant experience fragments. An execution agent can inspect these fragments and their referenced capabilities, while reflection separates concrete execution evidence from reusable abstractions. We study the framework across four benchmarks, five evaluation settings, and three language model backbones. Across backbones, AppWorld Normal and Challenge task goal completion average 51.91 and 27.99, respectively, exceeding the baseline without memory by 6.99 and 4.99 percentage points. An AppWorld ablation associates directed connections with an additional improvement of 2.08 points over independent operation cards. The results motivate composition of reusable operations while exposing tradeoffs in retrieval overhead and conditions for valid reuse.

OpenDriveLab.title: FOMI: A Force-Feedback Manipulation Interface for Teaching Contact-Rich Manipulation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yishu Shen, Yiming Luo, Ruilin Wang, Bowen Yang, Shuai Yang
OpenDriveLab.summary: FOMI is a novel force-feedback interface that enhances robot-free collection of contact-rich demonstrations, improving efficiency and enabling effective teleoperation for manipulation tasks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Robot-free collection with handheld interfaces enables scalable acquisition of human demonstrations for policy learning. However, existing handheld interfaces often provide limited intuitive force feedback, making contact-rich demonstration collection challenging for human operators. To address this, we present FOMI, a force-feedback manipulation interface with a scissor-shaped mechanism, which transmits object interaction forces directly to the operator's hands through actuation links without force sensors. This intuitive force feedback supports real-time action adjustment during robot-free collection of contact-rich demonstrations. Around FOMI, we build a demonstration collection system that integrates sensor calibration, data acquisition, and synchronization for robot-free collection. By further mapping pose changes and gripper opening of FOMI to robot end-effector poses and gripper commands, the system also supports teleoperation. Across four contact-rich tasks, FOMI improves collection efficiency by approximately 29% and 18% over the best baselines in robot-free collection and teleoperation, respectively. Demonstrations collected with FOMI in both modes enable policies to perform challenging contact-rich manipulation tasks with high success rates.

OpenDriveLab.title: Designing Textual Interfaces To Enhance Llm Reasoning On Audio-Visual Question Answering
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yi Wang, Tianzi Wang, Tong Lei, Dahan Wang, Peter Bell
OpenDriveLab.summary: This paper explores how different textual interface designs impact prompt optimization for audio-visual question answering in multimodal reasoning systems, revealing trade-offs in interpretability and optimization difficulty.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers. We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. We compare three interface designs, including a direct inference system consisting of a single omni-modal large language model (OmniLLM), a captioner-reasoner system, and an agentic architecture in which a primary agent orchestrates subagent OmniLLMs. Experiments with Qwen3-Omni and Gemini show that direct prompt optimization provides model-dependent gains; the captioner-reasoner system and the agentic system expose more interpretable optimization interfaces but are harder to optimize, where error analysis of cases affected by optimization is conducted. Our study highlights textual interface design as an important factor in making prompt optimization effective for omni-modal reasoning systems. Our implementation details are specified in GitHub repo.

OpenDriveLab.title: Towards Agentic Robots: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Chonghan Qin, Dongming Wu, Kaituo Feng, Jiaxu Wang, Xinlei Yu
OpenDriveLab.summary: This paper outlines the evolving concept of agentic robots, categorizing research into four domains while addressing challenges and future directions for enhancing robotic intelligence and adaptability.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.

OpenDriveLab.title: KineWorld: Action-Induced Transport Fields for Embodied World Modeling
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Ziying Song, Yuchen Liu, Zhuoran Xu, Ziyang Liu, Jian Jin
OpenDriveLab.summary: KineWorld introduces a transport-aware framework for embodied world modeling, enhancing action prediction by aligning visual generation with critical spatial changes in robot interactions.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Embodied world models predict the visual consequences of candidate actions before execution. However, existing action-conditioned world models often adopt uniformly weighted visual generation objectives that can be misaligned with embodied prediction needs. Even with explicit motion conditioning, these objectives can underemphasize spatially sparse changes that are critical to interaction. We propose KineWorld, a transport-aware world-modeling framework that extends robot kinematics from motion conditioning to the spatial allocation of generative supervision. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) constructs renderer-derived, camera-aligned transport fields from commanded robot motion. Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates their motion support on the video-latent grid and reweights future-RGB flow matching through a normalized mixture of uniform and transport-focused distributions. We train KineWorld using ALOHA-AgileX bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0. KineWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 68.95 in single-view evaluation and a TWB-Score of 54.82 in multi-view evaluation. These results support a shift from appearance fitting toward action-consequence modeling for embodied decision-making.

OpenDriveLab.title: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Jingjing Wei, Hao Zhao, Xinke Li, Linxi Yu, Xiaosong Gao
OpenDriveLab.summary: The MathVis benchmark evaluates LLMs' diagram-assisted reasoning in math problem visualization, revealing limitations in their ability to produce clear, visually coherent outputs.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Through rigorous evaluation, GPT-6-Astra, Claude Fable 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%, respectively. We found that although the tasks require visualization, LLMs produce outputs dominated by formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs, rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.

OpenDriveLab.title: ReAT: Residual Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Robot Policies
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Dijia Zhan, Zhuo Li, Xuemiao Xu, Sun Zheng, Jinyi Li
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper presents Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), enhancing autoregressive robot policies by enabling tokens to iteratively refine action reconstructions, improving performance across various tasks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.

OpenDriveLab.title: EndoRSI: Physical-Evidence-Driven Recursive Improvement of Endoscopic Robot Policies
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Chi Kit Ng, Yidong Zhang, Tianchun Wu, Siu Hing Lui, Hanlin Zhao
OpenDriveLab.summary: EndoRSI is a self-improving robotic system that refines endoscopic policies through iterative physical experimentation and human oversight, significantly enhancing insertion success rates.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Artificial intelligence is beginning to automate scientific discovery, yet physical robot-policy research still relies on scientists and engineers to interpret experimental failures and decide how controllers should be revised. We present EndoRSI (Endoscopic Recursive Self-Improvement), a human-governed, self-improving robotic research system in which the embedded EndoForge coding agent iteratively develops and refines endoscopic robot policies using evidence from physical experiments. Physical execution remains isolated within a safety-constrained runtime under human authorisation. In motorised endoscopy, validation evidence first caused the agent to reject an initial action representation, while subsequent physical experiments falsified an offline-supported insertion strategy by revealing hazardous closed-loop behaviour absent from the source data. Failed physical rollouts were then incorporated into policy revision; insertion success subsequently increased from 2/21 in the first generation to 17/21 in the fourth. The frozen final policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and was the best performing autonomous policy across six independent ex-vivo porcine specimens. These results show that physical robot interaction can serve as experimental evidence for agent-driven robot policy research.

OpenDriveLab.title: SimVTA: Simulation-Grounded Video-Trajectory Alignment for Driving World Action Models
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Changhui Jing, Haochen Tian, Hongchen Li, Tianyu Li, Caojun Wang
OpenDriveLab.summary: SimVTA enhances driving world action models by integrating simulation-grounded video supervision for trajectory optimization, significantly improving planning performance in real-world scenarios.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Driving world action models (WAMs) learn from paired trajectories and future observations. Post-training with reinforcement learning allows the policy to explore alternative trajectories and improve planning using driving rewards. However, driving logs contain future videos only for the recorded trajectories, leaving these alternatives without corresponding visual supervision. Thus, we introduce SimVTA, a simulation-grounded post-training framework that combines trajectory optimization with video supervision. First, we sample candidate trajectories for each observation and use a real-world simulator (e.g., World Engine) to render future videos for high-reward candidates in real-world scenes reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). This provides trajectory-matched supervision independent of the model's own predictions. Under a limited rendering budget, we prioritize video supervision for higher-error futures among these rendered candidates. Finally, we optimize trajectory planning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and use a flow-matching loss on the matched videos to update shared representations. At inference time, the model predicts trajectories directly, without simulator calls. On NAVSIM v1, applying SimVTA to a WAM initialization improves PDMS from 86.2 to 91.3 (+5.1). It achieves 88.2 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and an average HD-Score of 38.8 in closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM. Ablations show that updating shared representations with video supervision improves planning, while prioritizing higher-error futures among high-reward trajectories further improves performance.

OpenDriveLab.title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Jingwei Song, Zhisheng Chen, Bingfan Zeng, Jing Tang, Yubo Hou
OpenDriveLab.summary: MC-EvoBench is a controlled Minecraft benchmark designed to evaluate and audit the transferability and durability of embodied capabilities in self-improving agents.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source-target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source

OpenDriveLab.title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yuhong Liu, Shenxi Wu, Junyi Chi, Beichen Zhang, Xuanlang Dai
OpenDriveLab.summary: SpatialASM enhances Large Vision-Language Models by integrating Active Spatial Mentalization through training-time spatial simulation, improving their spatial reasoning capabilities across multiple benchmarks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? We term this ability Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM), an intrinsic component of visual intelligence that remains substantially underdeveloped in current LVLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SpatialASM, a scalable framework to internalize ASM into LVLMs through training-time spatial simulation. SpatialASM employs an allocentric novel-view generator to ground hypothetical viewpoints in visual evidence and produces two complementary forms of supervision: i) explicit ASM trajectories that teach LVLMs when and how to adaptively invoke view planning and imagination during spatial reasoning, and ii) automatically-constructed perspective-taking tasks that further strengthens viewpoint-conditioned scene imagination. On seven benchmarks spanning relatively perception-oriented spatial understanding to more challenging tasks requiring multi-image, cross-view and viewpoint-transformation reasoning, SpatialASM yields performance gain on LVLMs of four LVLM backbones in spatial reasoning while retaining their original general vision capabilities. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves average accuracy across the seven spatial benchmarks. And the synthesis of ASM trajectories provides a scalable pathway to alleviate the scarcity of spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision for eliciting active viewpoint exploration and mental scene simulation.

OpenDriveLab.title: SAP-CoPE: Social-Aware Planning using Cooperative Pose Estimation with Infrastructure Sensor Nodes
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Minghao Ning, Yufeng Yang, Shucheng Huang, Jiaming Zhong, Keqi Shu
OpenDriveLab.summary: SAP-CoPE is an indoor navigation framework that combines cooperative sensing, human pose estimation, and social-aware motion planning to enhance robot interactions in human-populated environments.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Autonomous mobile robots must operate smoothly in human-populated indoor environments, where onboard-only sensing suffers from limited perception range and occlusions, and socially compliant motion planning must account for human psychological comfort zones. These factors complicate accurate recognition of human intentions and the generation of comfortable, social-aware trajectories. To address these challenges, we propose SAP-CoPE, an indoor navigation framework that integrates cooperative infrastructure sensing, human pose estimation, and a social-aware MPC planner. In the perception module, an uncertainty-aware optimization problem is formulated to estimate 3D human poses from camera observations, with optional incorporation of sparse LiDAR point-cloud measurements, while considering human joint coherence. In the planning module, the estimated human pose and orientation are used to construct a personal-space (PS) field within an MPC framework, enabling the robot to account for both physical safety and psychological comfort. Extensive real-world evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in generating social-aware trajectories for autonomous systems.

OpenDriveLab.title: Latent Reward Steering: An Adaptive Inference-Time Framework that Implicitly Promotes Cognitive Behaviors in Reasoning LLMs
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Jiakang Li, Guanyu Zhu, Can Jin, Chenxi Huang, Dexu Yu
OpenDriveLab.summary: Latent Reward Steering (LRS) enhances reasoning in LLMs by adaptively optimizing latent states based on reward signals, improving cognitive behavior deployment during inference.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Strong reasoning depends not only on model knowledge but also on how effectively cognitive behaviors are deployed during generation. Existing methods often rely on explicit behavior-level control, making them insufficiently adaptive when failures and required corrections vary across reasoning states, tasks, and models. To this end, we propose Latent Reward Steering (LRS), an adaptive inference-time framework that promotes cognitive behaviors by optimizing the sparse-autoencoder (SAE) latent states that implicitly carry them. Rather than relying on predefined cognitive behaviors or steering directions derived from them, LRS trains a latent reward model on reasoning traces by final answer correctness to estimate the quality of intermediate latent states. During inference, reward gradients provide state-specific correction directions for fragile latent states, while a reward and confidence gate restricts intervention to states the reward signal flags as fragile. Experiments on multiple reasoning LLM backbones and benchmarks show that \ours consistently improves performance over various baselines, and post-hoc analyses further indicate that \ours implicitly promotes good cognitive behaviors that fix the original reasoning errors. Code is available at: https://github.com/jiakanglee/Latent-Reward-Steering.

OpenDriveLab.title: Object Concepts Emerge from Motion
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Boshi Li, Xiaohui Wang, Xiaoyang Wu, Zhichao Li, Ya Yang
OpenDriveLab.summary: This paper introduces a motion-based framework for learning object-centric visual representations from videos, achieving superior performance in various tasks without requiring human annotations.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Object-centric visual representations are important for physical-world perception, but existing visual pretraining methods often capture semantic categories without preserving the identity and coherence of individual instances. We present a biologically inspired framework that learns object-centric representations for single images from raw videos. Our approach uses motion boundaries as a source of object-level grouping: off-the-shelf optical flow and clustering produce pseudo-instance masks, which supervise a single-image encoder with pixel-level pairwise metric learning. The framework requires neither human annotations nor camera calibration. We first obtain 195 million pseudo-labeled frames from 7,163 hours of driving and web videos, then expand the supervision to 421 million frames with Motion-Verified Self-Training, which combines model proposals with motion evidence. We train encoders up to Swin-H and distill the learned representations into a family of Swin backbones. Across monocular depth estimation, 3D object detection, 3D occupancy prediction, and end-to-end planning, the resulting models achieve competitive or superior performance relative to supervised and self-supervised pretraining baselines, with particularly strong transfer on geometry- and instance-sensitive tasks. These results show that motion-derived supervision can teach static image encoders to represent visual instances, providing a complementary direction for scalable visual pretraining.

OpenDriveLab.title: MIRAGE: Metric Inference and Reliability-Aware Gaussian Estimation from Feed-Forward Vision
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Xinzhe Wang, Changjian Jiang, Kaiwen Song, Xudong Li, Kerui Ren
OpenDriveLab.summary: MIRAGE integrates feed-forward visual geometry with LiDAR-IMU data for accurate metric pose estimation and high-fidelity Gaussian reconstruction, outperforming existing vision-only methods.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Feed-forward 3D priors enable high-quality reconstruction from image streams but often lack reliable metric scale and suffer from long-term trajectory drift. In contrast, LiDAR--inertial estimation provides metrically accurate motion but lacks the image-space consistency needed for high-fidelity reconstruction. We propose $MIRAGE$, which anchors feed-forward visual geometry to LiDAR--IMU metric motion and regulates online pose corrections according to correspondence support and cross-modal agreement, jointly enabling accurate metric pose estimation and high-fidelity Gaussian reconstruction. Experiments on Oxford Spires, M2DGR and INS show that MIRAGE achieves accurate metric trajectory estimation, outperforming COLMAP, a widely used but computationally expensive reference for vision-only benchmarks. Motivated by the scarcity of long-horizon monocular benchmarks for large-scale indoor reconstruction, we further build a multimodal data-collection platform and use MIRAGE to establish accurate 6-DoF reference trajectories for a new vision-only benchmark. We benchmark recent monocular large-scale reconstruction methods on this dataset, providing a systematic evaluation of their performance in long-horizon indoor scenes.

OpenDriveLab.title: EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Jie Huang, Yanan Chen, Ruixun Liu, Kaichen He, Xinyi He
OpenDriveLab.summary: EmbodiedCLBench is a novel benchmark for assessing continual learning in self-evolving agents within embodied environments, revealing limitations and insights into skill transfer and task complexity.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.

OpenDriveLab.title: PartiGen: Part-Aware Representations for Language-Conditioned Humanoid Motion Generation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Chuxuan Huang, Zhanxiang Cao, Tianyue Zhan, Haoyang Li, Yang Zhang
OpenDriveLab.summary: PartiGen is a part-aware framework that generates humanoid motion from language by integrating anatomical structure and improving kinematic consistency, achieving significant performance enhancements in simulation and real execution.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Translating language into humanoid motion requires coordinating body parts, determining motion duration, and producing references suitable for robot execution. We introduce PartiGen, a part-aware latent diffusion framework that incorporates anatomical structure into a shared whole-body motion representation. Part-specific attention processes anatomically masked frame features, and its outputs are fused to combine local limb information with whole-body context. Conditioned on text and motion history, the model generates motion primitives autoregressively. Forward-kinematics supervision encourages kinematic consistency, while a learned end-of-sequence predictor selects a frame-level endpoint after generation. On HumanML3D retargeted to the Unitree G1, PartiGen achieves a segment-level FID of 3.165, a 16.8% reduction over TextOp, and improves R@1 by 1.4 percentage points. In the duration study with 16-frame primitives, endpoint prediction reduces mean absolute duration error from 12.471 to 3.080 frames compared with a fixed-length cutoff. We further evaluate robot execution using a pretrained, frozen GRIT tracker: 409 of 500 generated references (81.8%) pass the posture-based stability screen in MuJoCo. Following simulation screening and manual selection, 26 of 27 attempted motions are judged successful on the real G1.

OpenDriveLab.title: OmniHOI: Dexterous Hand-Object Interaction from Monocular Human Video
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Ting Mao, Yanming Shao, Ziheng Wang, Haoyu Liu, Yiqun Wang
OpenDriveLab.summary: OmniHOI is a novel pipeline that converts monocular human manipulation videos into accurate dexterous hand-object interaction trajectories, achieving significantly improved success rates over previous methods.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Monocular videos of human manipulation provide abundant dexterous demonstrations, yet reconstructing hand-object interaction from a single view and transferring it to robot hands remain difficult, limiting their direct use for robot execution. Prior methods either require task-specific RL training, limiting scalability, or assume clean motion-capture trajectories and thus cannot operate directly on video. We present OmniHOI, a pipeline that turns an RGB video of hand-object interaction into an interaction-faithful trajectory on dexterous hands. The key idea is to enforce physical consistency using the evidence available at each stage: image evidence during reconstruction, contact geometry during retargeting, and dynamics during physics-in-the-loop refinement. Each stage optimizes the corresponding representation directly, correcting errors before they propagate downstream or must be absorbed by a learned policy. Across 150 motion-capture trajectories transferred to each of five dexterous hands with 6 to 22 DoF, we achieve 39-89% success, compared with at most 31% for prior transfer methods. On 60 monocular video clips, we achieve 53% success, compared with 28% for the best prior video-to-robot pipeline. Its trajectories also execute on a real bimanual robot across diverse tasks.

OpenDriveLab.title: TKCAM: Text and Keyframe to Camera Trajectory Generation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Haozhe Yang, Zhiyang Dou, Zekai Gu, Cheng Lin, Wenping Wang
OpenDriveLab.summary: TKCAM is a novel framework for generating controllable camera trajectories using text and keyframe inputs, outperforming existing methods in various evaluation metrics.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Generating high-quality and controllable camera motion is essential for AI-assisted cinematography, video synthesis, and 3D scene understanding. We introduce TKCAM, a Text- and Keyframe-conditioned CAMera-motion synthesis framework based on generative masked modeling. We represent camera dynamics using a 12-dimensional kinematic feature comprising position, velocity, and a continuous rotation representation and discretize them into hierarchical motion tokens via a Residual Vector Quantizer (RVQ). A two-stage masked transformer architecture then learns to reconstruct and refine these tokens, utilizing explicit self- and cross-attention modules for multimodal conditioning. A central feature of our framework is sparse visual keyframe conditioning: users can provide free-form text prompts together with RGB observations at selected timestamps, which provide temporally localized visual guidance for generating coherent in-between trajectories. Furthermore, to advance evaluation standards, we curate RealEstate10K-Cap, a large-scale text-camera dataset, and establish a cross-domain benchmark with a Universal CLaTr Evaluator. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TKCAM surpasses recent state-of-the-art baselines on Fréchet distance (FID), text-motion matching scores, and retrieval metrics (R@K), while additional analyses evaluate temporal smoothness and cross-domain generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/linearalgebrayhz/TKCAM.

OpenDriveLab.title: Autogenesis: A Self-Evolving Agent Protocol
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Wentao Zhang, Zhe Zhao, Haibin Wen, Yingcheng Wu, Cankun Guo
OpenDriveLab.summary: The Autogenesis Protocol (AGP) enables self-evolving agent systems to manage heterogeneous updates through a structured lifecycle, enhancing performance across various benchmarks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: LLM-based agent systems can adapt by revising prompts, constructing tools, and changing other runtime resources. Managing these heterogeneous updates requires a shared lifecycle for identifying targets, assessing candidates, and retaining accepted versions, complementing communication protocols such as A2A and MCP. We introduce AUTOGENESIS PROTOCOL (AGP), which decouples what evolves from how updates are proposed. Its Resource Substrate Protocol Layer (RSPL) represents prompts, agents, tools, environments, and memory as protocol-registered resources with explicit state and versioned interfaces. Its Self-Evolution Protocol Layer (SEPL) specifies candidate proposal, assessment, and commit, with auditable histories and support for restoring retained resource states. We instantiate AGP in AUTOGENESIS SYSTEM (AGS), a self-evolving multi-agent system that retrieves, instantiates, and refines resources during execution. Across reasoning, tool-use, and coding benchmarks, AGS improves over its non-evolving configuration, and repeated reasoning runs report the accompanying output-token cost. Execution cases show a shared update lifecycle across all five resource types.

OpenDriveLab.title: Self-Evolving Spatial Reasoning in Vision Language Models via Geometric Logic Consistency
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Junming Liu, Yuqi Li, Yifei Sun, Maonan Wang, Yiming Cheng
OpenDriveLab.summary: The SAGE framework enhances spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models by integrating geometric logic consistency and self-evolution, improving robustness and generalization across transformations.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have made striking progress, yet their spatial reasoning remains fragile. Models that answer an original input correctly can still fail under valid transformations with predictable answer mappings, revealing a gap between instance-level correctness and robust spatial reasoning. To address this, we propose Spatial Alignment via Geometric Evolution (SAGE), a self-evolving framework that improves robust spatial reasoning through geometric and linguistic duality operations. SAGE incorporates duality consistency into GRPO training, encouraging models to produce coherent answers across original and transformed inputs. SAGE co-evolves duality generation and solution, allowing the model to continually expose and address its own reasoning weaknesses. A dynamic operation pool identifies challenging operations and retires mastered ones, keeping training focused on informative duality signals. SAGE is model-agnostic, data-efficient compared to prior post-training methods, and can be applied as a lightweight adaptation stage to any existing VLM. Experiments on video and spatial reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines and enhanced generalization to unseen data.

OpenDriveLab.title: Environmental Feedback Modeling Matters: Rethinking Feedback Treatment in Agentic Hindsight Self-Distillation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Hangxi Guo, Fengyuan Liu, Yue Wang, Yuhua Qi, Haoyi Xiong
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper introduces SELF, a framework that enhances reinforcement learning by optimizing environmental feedback modeling alongside hindsight self-distillation, significantly improving agent performance.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Reinforcement learning is commonly used to train language agents in interactive environments, but cannot be directly applied when rewards are unavailable. Recent methods use environmental feedback as privileged context for hindsight self-distillation, but our analysis suggests that simply conditioning the teacher on feedback is insufficient, motivating us to rethink how environmental feedback is used in agentic self-distillation. Given that environmental feedback contains rich supervision for modeling how the environment responds to agent actions, we introduce \textit{agentic SElf-distilLation with environmental Feedback modeling} (SELF), a framework that jointly optimizes environmental feedback modeling and hindsight self-distillation. SELF learns to predict environmental responses while distilling guidance from a feedback-conditioned self-teacher into the policy. Our analysis reveals a mutually reinforcing mechanism: environmental feedback modeling strengthens hindsight supervision and policy learning, while self-distillation enhances the model's ability to model environmental feedback. With Qwen3-8B, SELF outperforms SDPO and GRPO by 6.4 and 4.1 percentage points in $τ$-bench success rate, and by 10.71 and 3.57 percentage points in AppWorld task goal completion, respectively. These results show that SELF uses environmental feedback more effectively within agentic self-distillation, improving agent capabilities.

OpenDriveLab.title: Fed-GRPO: Reward-Signal-Driven Federated Group Relative Policy Optimization
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Pengxin Guo, Shuang Zeng, Zonggen Li, Weiying Zheng, Mengting Liu
OpenDriveLab.summary: Fed-GRPO is a federated training framework for reinforcement learning that optimizes collaboration without data sharing, enhancing performance while significantly reducing communication costs.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong reasoning capabilities when fine-tuned with reinforcement learning (RL), particularly through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). However, existing GRPO methods assume centralized access to training data, which may not hold in practice due to privacy or regulatory constraints. To this end, we propose Fed-GRPO, a federated GRPO training framework that addresses these privacy constraints by enabling collaborative reasoning training without sharing raw data, which leverages the reward statistics naturally produced during GRPO training as zero-cost signals to guide aggregation, local training, and communication. Fed-GRPO contains three reward-signal-driven mechanisms: (i) \emph{signal-weighted aggregation} that weights clients by their reward standard deviation, prioritizing clients with stronger learning signals; (ii) \emph{global reward calibration} that re-weights per-prompt objectives based on the local-global reward gap, steering each client toward its relative weaknesses; and (iii) \emph{adaptive sparse communication} that allocates bandwidth based on the informativeness of each client's update. Extensive experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks demonstrate that Fed-GRPO achieves the best performance among all federated methods, clearly outperforms FedAvg and approaches centralized training performance, while losslessly reducing communication by $32\times$ and supporting up to $621\times$ compression under tight bandwidth budgets with only graceful accuracy degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/HKU-HealthAI/Fed-GRPO.

OpenDriveLab.title: YOCO: You Only Calibrate Once! Fast Mocap Calibration for Dexterous Teleoperation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yu Zhang, Yunqi Li, Yushi Du, Yi Ma, Yanchao Yang
OpenDriveLab.summary: YOCO is a novel calibration framework that enhances hand-pose estimation in dexterous teleoperation by efficiently correcting biases without requiring user-specific model training.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Dexterous teleoperation requires reliable human-hand state estimations. However, common low-cost motion-capture gloves and markerless trackers often exhibit biases that vary across users, glove fit, and recording sessions, degrading retargeting and demonstration quality. We present YOCO, a fast few-shot, fine-tuning-free calibration framework that corrects biased hand-pose streams from a small set of paired raw and target poses. Instead of optimizing a separate model for every operator or session, YOCO conditions a calibration HyperNet on the paired examples and predicts LoRA-style updates for a frozen MANO hand-estimation module, turning per-user calibration into a lightweight feed-forward adaptation step while preserving the geometric prior of MANO and the efficiency of a compact estimator. We train YOCO with synthetic drift augmentations on InterHand2.6M and evaluate on augmented InterHand sequences, offline real glove data, and dexterous teleoperation tasks. Across these settings, YOCO improves calibration efficiency, hand-state estimation quality and teleoperation performance compared with uncalibrated input and standard calibration baselines.

OpenDriveLab.title: Can Jev be Your Q or Policy in Reinforcement Learning?
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yi Ma, Tianpei Yang, Yaodong Yang, Weixun Wang, Hongyao Tang
OpenDriveLab.summary: This paper demonstrates that Jev, a decision model, enhances reinforcement learning performance and sample efficiency by serving as a reference policy, exploration judge, and replay rater.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Foundation models supply reinforcement learning (RL) with priors that mitigate its longstanding weaknesses in sample efficiency and transfer, but their token-by-token generation makes queries sequential and costly. Jev, a recently released decision model, generates nothing and returns calibrated, typed answers in a single forward pass. Existing work studies foundation models in RL either as models to be trained or as generators to be prompted, and Jev belongs to neither category, having so far served only as a black box in single domains. How well such a model decides on its own in RL environments, and how it can improve RL as a component of training, therefore remain unaddressed. To this end, in this paper we first examine the requirements that the objects of an RL system place on the answers they consume, and establish that Jev can fulfill all of them except the cardinal use of a value function. The remaining objects form positions that admit several roles each. We then construct algorithms that employ Jev at three of these positions, as a reference policy, an exploration judge, and a replay rater, to improve sample efficiency, exploration, and learning performance. Across nine MiniGrid tasks and three Atari games, training with Jev outperforms a standard RL learner, including where the learner makes no progress alone, while the model itself remains untrained. To our knowledge, we present the first use of Jev within the RL learning process and establish a frozen decision model as a usable component of RL training, inviting further exploration of how Jev and other advanced decision models can improve RL.

OpenDriveLab.title: Seek-and-View Reasoning for Multi-View Spatial Understanding
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Qixiang Chen, Cheng Zhang, Fucai Ke, Chi-Wing Fu, Jianfei Cai
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper introduces Vantage, a model-agnostic framework that enhances multi-view spatial reasoning by integrating viewpoint-grounded analysis with geometry-grounded evidence synthesis, improving performance across various benchmarks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Existing approaches to multi-view spatial reasoning operate largely on sparse input views. Vision-language models (VLMs) are thus restricted to understand a scene and infer spatial relations within these fixed views, leading to fragile cross-view alignment and geometry-to-language bottleneck. To address these issues, we formulate a novel Seek-and-View reasoning approach to find implicit cross-view spatial evidence by locating a question-relevant view to support the spatial reasoning. To realize this approach, we propose Vantage, a training-free model-agnostic reasoning framework that pairs a VLM with a 3D foundation model: a viewpoint-grounded reasoning stage for question analysis and view planning, followed by a geometry-grounded evidence augmentation stage to effectively synthesize and incorporate visual evidence into the final reasoning. Comprehensive experiments on six VLMs demonstrate consistent improvements on five benchmarks without fine-tuning. Overall, by revealing spatial evidence through view-grounded reasoning, Vantage can largely reduce reliance on language-based cross-view alignment and improve multi-view spatial understanding. Our code is available at https://github.com/q1xiangchen/Vantage.

OpenDriveLab.title: Look Back, Think Ahead: Visual Memory on Demand for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yicheng Xue, Han Wu, Jufeng Yang, Minjing Dong, Xinghao Chen
OpenDriveLab.summary: ViMoD enhances multimodal reasoning efficiency by dynamically managing visual context through adaptive token aggregation and selective evidence retrieval, outperforming existing methods with minimal parameter increase.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Processing long visual token sequences from high-resolution images makes multi-step reasoning computationally expensive for multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Existing one-shot pruning and aggregation methods compress visual tokens into a fixed context before decoding. However, visual evidence needs can shift as reasoning unfolds, making it difficult for a fixed compressed context to retain all the details needed across stages. To address this challenge, we propose ViMoD, a lightweight framework that maintains a compact visual context while preserving access to original fine-grained evidence as reasoning needs evolve. Deformable Aggregation of Region-wise Tokens (DART) learns content-adaptive groups and aggregation capacities, constructing compact Coarse representations linked to recoverable original Fine tokens. Temporal Routing for Adaptive Contextual Evidence (TRACE) integrates decoding history to anticipate upcoming evidence needs and select, retain, or replace active Fine-token groups. Selected Fine tokens augment the persistent Coarse context in the frozen backbone, enabling stage-specific evidence access without continuously attending to all visual tokens. On Qwen3-VL-4B, ViMoD outperforms all evaluated baselines on all eight reasoning benchmarks at a 20% target visual token budget, improving the mean normalized score by 39.0% over the strongest evaluated one-shot baseline. These gains are achieved with only 0.0546% additional trainable parameters relative to the frozen backbone.

OpenDriveLab.title: ContourVLA: A Closed-Loop Perception-Action Contour Policy for Generalized Referring Expression Segmentation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Ruicheng Zhang, Kaiwen Shen, Jiaqi Hou, Shuhan Yang, Junchao Huang
OpenDriveLab.summary: ContourVLA introduces a closed-loop perception-action framework for generalized referring expression segmentation, enhancing boundary precision and multimodal feature adaptation, outperforming existing methods significantly.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Generalized referring expression segmentation (GRES) requires dynamically balancing high-level semantics for identifying a variable number of language-specified referents with fine-grained visual evidence for precise boundary delineation. This requirement challenges existing cascaded vision-language architectures, which typically rely on static feature interfaces and single-pass mask prediction, limiting adaptive perception and geometric correction. We introduce ContourVLA, a vision-language-action policy that recasts GRES as a closed-loop visuomotor process, in which editable contours serve as explicit policy states that condition multimodal perception and are updated by geometric action chunks. Evolution-Aware Semantic Scheduling (EASS) couples contour-guided bidirectional boundary sampling with state-conditioned routing of multilevel multimodal features, adapting perception to each contour state. Following supervised initialization, Dustbin-Augmented Entropic Credit Transport GRPO (DECT-GRPO) jointly optimizes discrete grounding and continuous contour actions with instance-level credits. Its rollout rewards and credits are derived from soft prediction-target correspondences that account for false positives and missed targets. ContourVLA improves gIoU over the strongest evaluated baselines by 8.7, 2.8, and 2.7 points on gRefCOCO val, testA, and testB, respectively, and achieves the highest mIoU across all eight RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg splits.

OpenDriveLab.title: RESETTLE: Robotic Recovery through Disagreement-Triggered Retrieval and Efficient Corrective Control
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yuxin Chen, Senqiao Yang, Zixuan Wang, Jinhui Ye, Changsheng Lu
OpenDriveLab.summary: RESETTLE is a model-agnostic framework that enhances robotic recovery efficiency by triggering interventions based on action disagreement, significantly reducing latency and improving success rates across various tasks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires timely intervention to correct emerging deviations and restore progress after execution errors. However, recovery methods based on repeated vision-language reasoning or iterative online optimization can incur substantial latency, delaying intervention. To address these challenges, we introduce RESETTLE(Robotic rEcovery through diSagrEement-Triggered reTrievaL and Efficient Corrective Control), a model-agnostic framework that provides computationally efficient recovery at the action-execution interface of frozen robot policies. RESETTLE triggers recovery when two action proposals independently sampled under identical conditioning persistently disagree. It retrieves a same-task demonstration reference using an adapted V-JEPA encoder and combines a state-servo prior with a guarded visual residual to execute one corrective action without online trajectory optimization or additional vision-language reasoning, then returns control to the base policy. Across six base policies in simulation, RESETTLE achieves up to 8.70%, 6.28%, and 6.83% absolute success-rate gains on LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World, and RoboCasa Tabletop, respectively, with further improvements on four real-world tasks using two policies. In QwenPI-based comparisons, its monitoring-and-recovery computation latency is 74.04%--93.57% lower than VoLoAgent's monitoring-and-planning latency for grasp and place tool calls. It also raises Harness VLA's LIBERO-Pro Swap success from 42% to 50%, demonstrating compatibility with high-level agentic planning. Code available at: https://github.com/JIA-Lab-research/RESETTLE

OpenDriveLab.title: DVD: Dynamic Vector Decoding for Efficient MLLM-based Perception
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Jinghua Hou, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
OpenDriveLab.summary: The DVD method enhances MLLM-based perception by transforming diverse 2D and 3D representations into compact 1D vector sequences, reducing token overhead and improving performance.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Multimodal large language models have made remarkable progress in bridging vision and language, facilitating various perception tasks essential for human-machine interaction, robotics, and autonomous driving. However, existing MLLM-based perception methods predominantly rely on text-based coordinate representation, which suffers from excessive token overhead, or fixed-range quantization, which suffers from range and precision constraints, especially for 3D domains with unbounded spatial range and high localization accuracy requirements. To address these challenges, we propose a dynamic vector decoding method named DVD, which unifies the representation of 2D and 3D perception tasks. Specifically, we first transform diverse perceptual representation (i.e., 2D bounding boxes, 2D masks, and 3D bounding boxes) into 1D vector sequences, which are then mapped to compact discrete tokens in the high-dimensional space. Then, a lightweight de-tokenizer enables seamless integration with MLLMs by decoding output tokens back to original 2D and 3D perceptual representations. Extensive experiments on 2D and 3D perception benchmarks including RefCOCO series, SUN-RGBD, KITTI, Hypersim, nuScenes demonstrate that DVD achieves superior performance in 2D and 3D tasks and reduces significantly the token overhead and inference latency. DVD provides an efficient and general framework for integrating perception capabilities into MLLMs, overcoming the inherent limitations of existing methods.

OpenDriveLab.title: RiCo: Neural Simulation of Rigid-Body Interactions via Local Contact Reasoning
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Ruixiang Ouyang, Guanren Qiao, Fansen Meng, Yueci Deng, Ruixing Jin
OpenDriveLab.summary: RiCo introduces a local contact reasoning approach for simulating rigid-body interactions, enhancing accuracy and fidelity by focusing on nearby surface interactions while reducing computational costs.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Accurate simulation of rigid-body interactions is essential for predictive physical world models. Despite recent progress in modeling object dynamics, capturing how local contacts between surfaces shape object motion remains challenging. While end-to-end world models predict interactions across entire scenes or objects, in practice, rigid-body contact is inherently local, and only nearby surfaces can directly exchange contact forces. Motivated by this observation, we introduce Rigid-body Contact Reasoning (RiCo), which represents interactions between objects through sparse neighborhoods of contact surface points. RiCo combines each point's state with the relative geometry, motion, and physical properties of nearby surfaces, then reasons across the object's points to determine how these local contacts jointly affect its motion. By confining cross-object reasoning to nearby surfaces while propagating contact information within each rigid body, RiCo retains fine-grained interaction details without the cost of modeling every pair of scene points. Such properties enable RiCo a higher accuracy and contact fidelity. Experiments on MOVi-benchmark demonstrate that RiCo reduces 100-frame position and orientation errors by 31-35% and approximately 38%, respectively, compared with baselines. Moreover, RiCo achieves high contact fidelity, with ground-truth-relative penetration-time and mean-depth differences of 11.0% and 2.22 mm, respectively. RiCo further generalizes zero-shot from small-scale training scenarios to scenes containing 270 objects. Our real-world multi-ball collision experiments further provide preliminary evidence of sim-to-real transfer.

OpenDriveLab.title: VersaCamVLA: Camera-Configurable VLA Policies for Robotic Manipulation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Boyao Han, Chen Shi, Jingjing Qian, ZhuoTan Tian, Li Jiang
OpenDriveLab.summary: VersaCamVLA introduces a flexible framework for robotic manipulation that adapts Vision-Language-Action models to variable camera configurations, enhancing robustness and performance across diverse settings.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful foundations for robotic manipulation, but their reliance on fixed camera configurations during training makes them brittle to changes in camera count or pose during deployment. To overcome these limitations, we propose VersaCamVLA, a camera-configurable framework that decouples camera-set representation from action learning. VersaCamVLA learns a unified scene-token interface that maps an arbitrary, variable set of posed RGB views into fixed-size latent scene tokens. This is achieved via multi-signal target-view prediction and Wrist-Augmented Pose Sampling (WAPS), which leverages natural wrist-camera motion for free pose diversity. At deployment, a lightweight spatial encoder injects these compact scene tokens into a pretrained base VLA as a supplementary visual condition, requiring no explicit 3D sensing or novel-view rendering. Experiments on RoboTwin, LIBERO, and a real-robot platform demonstrate that VersaCamVLA consistently outperforms prior VLA methods and direct multi-view baselines, maintaining robust performance across varying camera counts and unseen camera poses.

OpenDriveLab.title: TAP3D: Thermal-Assisted 3D Human Point Clouds
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Xie Zhang, Chengxiao Li, Xuan Liu, Chenshu Wu
OpenDriveLab.summary: TAP3D introduces a novel system that reconstructs 3D human point clouds from thermal signatures, enhancing accuracy, cost-effectiveness, and privacy in human sensing applications.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Human body point clouds are a versatile representation for AI-enabled human sensing. However, existing methods using LiDAR, radar, and depth cameras suffer from inherent drawbacks in high cost, sparse reconstruction, and privacy concerns, etc. In this paper, we exploit low-cost thermal arrays and present TAP3D, the first system to reconstruct 3D human point clouds from body heat signatures, offering significant advantages in cost, density, human sensitivity, and privacy. To overcome major challenges in depth estimation, thermal interference, and multi-person separation, we propose a novel physics-informed design, which integrates a forward thermal physics model with two distinct modules: multi-primitive estimation for self-supervised joint recovery of depth and other thermal properties, and geometric perspective fusion for suppressing interference and disentangling multiple people. We implement TAP3D using a single commodity thermal array sensor and build a large-scale dataset (160K samples, 8 environments, 11 users) for evaluation. TAP3D achieves remarkable accuracy for dense point cloud generation, enabling downstream tasks like fall detection (91.46%), indoor tracking (21.86 cm MAE), and human mesh recovery (4.87 cm error). By transforming body heat into point clouds for the first time, TAP3D pioneers a new paradigm for privacy-first, fully passive human sensing for many applications. TAP3D is open-sourced at https://github.com/aiot-lab/TAP3D.

OpenDriveLab.title: RoboAug: One Annotation to Hundreds of Scenes via Region-Contrastive Data Augmentation for Robotic Manipulation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Xinhua Wang, Kun Wu, Zhen Zhao, Hu Cao, Yinuo Zhao
OpenDriveLab.summary: RoboAug introduces a generative data augmentation framework requiring minimal supervision to enhance robotic manipulation generalization across diverse environments, outperforming existing methods in real-world tests.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Enhancing the generalization of robotic learning in diverse unseen environments remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches often rely on large-scale pretraining, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming, or semantic data augmentation methods that assume flawless upstream object detection in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose RoboAug, a novel generative data augmentation framework that reduces reliance on large-scale pretraining and perfect visual recognition by requiring only a single image with bounding box annotations for dataset construction. Leveraging this minimal supervision, RoboAug employs pretrained generative models for precise semantic augmentation and introduces a plug-and-play region-contrastive loss to guide attention toward task-relevant regions, thereby enhancing generalization and task success rates. Extensive real-world experiments on UR-5e, AgileX, and Tian Gong 2.0 demonstrate that RoboAug consistently outperforms state-of-the-art augmentation baselines under background, distractor, and lighting shifts. Our project is available at https://x-roboaug.github.io/.

OpenDriveLab.title: TACROSS: An Efficient and Low-Cost Scalable Human Touch System Across Heterogeneous Tactile Sensors for Dexterous Robot Learning
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Bo Chen, Huanzhang Hu, Junyang Ma, Bo Yue, Fangdi Yu
OpenDriveLab.summary: TACROSS is a low-cost, scalable system that aligns human tactile data with robotic sensors for efficient learning in dexterous manipulation tasks, achieving significant cost and efficiency improvements.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Collecting tactile demonstrations on robots is costly and slow, motivating the use of lower-cost human tactile gloves for scalable data collection. However, human capacitive/piezoresistive gloves and robotic tactile sensors differ fundamentally in transduction principle, sensor layout, spatial resolution, and dynamic response, making alignment of raw sensor channels ill-posed. To address this problem, we present TACROSS, a scalable system for learning from human touch and transferring it to robots that bridges this heterogeneity by aligning tactile streams at the level of contact events rather than raw sensor values. The hardware component of TACROSS integrates a piezoresistive glove with five layers and a cost of USD 10.86 with 285 sensing points.
